primary_reviews.rationale: Collation is clean here: every original-language slice this row prints sits at byte tier against the verse its own prose names. The Hebrew also backs the span — but not by the route the row takes to it. What actually holds Ezra.1.2 through Ezra.1.4 together as one quoted decree is unbroken directive modality: verse 3 runs a volitive chain יְהִ֤י … וְיַ֕עַל … וְיִ֗בֶן , and verse 4 continues that register with יְנַשְּׂא֨וּהוּ֙ , a piel imperfect carrying a third-person object suffix and directive force, so the speech has demonstrably not lapsed before the end of Ezra.1.4. That modality is interrupted at the wayyiqtol וַיָּק֜וּמוּ , which restarts narrated sequence under a new grammatical subject. The row instead nominates English punctuation as its closing warrant, and there the argument is unsupported: the pointed text carries no closing quotation formula of any kind, so nothing in the Hebrew answers to the mark cited. The opening frames are sound — the regnal time-frame, the infinitive-construct fulfilment phrase, the proclamation formula, and the messenger formula at Ezra.1.2 are all correctly identified and correctly quoted.

challenges.claim: The stated close warrant is tier-4 metadata: the rationale says the speech ends 'where WEB's closing single quote mark ends' at web:Ezra.1.4. Translator punctuation is a modern editorial convention and cannot bound a unit under the campaign's evidence rules. A tier-1 warrant is available and unused: the jussive series יְהִ֤י , וְיַ֕עַל , וְיִ֗בֶן at oshb:Ezra.1.3 is carried forward by יְנַשְּׂא֨וּהוּ֙ at oshb:Ezra.1.4, and that directive modality is terminated by the wayyiqtol וַיָּק֜וּמוּ at oshb:Ezra.1.5 with a fresh subject. The boundary is right; the reason given for it is not admissible.
challenges.suggested_action: Keep the span as frozen and replace the quotation-mark sentence with the volitive-chain plus wayyiqtol-resumption warrant, which the row's own final sentence already half states.

primary_reviews.rationale: The row's opening and closing frames both hold up under direct testing. The regnal-year opener fused to the Jeremiah-fulfillment clause at 1:1 is a genuine tier-1 era-opener matching the strategy's own device list, and the proclamation frame hands cleanly into Cyrus's quoted words at 1:2. The quotation's own close at 1:4, followed by 1:5's subject pivot to the household heads, gives the unit a real edge rather than a chapter-shaped one; this also matches the strategy's explicit inset rule keeping the edict inside its 1:1-4 frame. The rejected alternative (folding through 1:11) is the right rival to name here, since separating 1:1's narration from 1:2-4's quotation is already foreclosed by the strategy's single-frame reading and is not a live option.

v1's boundary_rationale swaps the closing-edge warrant from WEB's quotation-mark closure to a Hebrew volitive-chain / wayyiqtol-cutoff argument, and explicitly disclaims the old warrant: the edict's edges are set 'not [by] chapter or verse numbering or WEB's punctuation.' But strongest_rejected_alternative was carried over unrepaired from v0 and still grounds the row's rejection of the coarser Ezra.1.1-Ezra.1.11 reading in 'the clean quotation-frame closure at Ezra.1.4' -- the very WEB-punctuation-adjacent warrant the repaired rationale just disclaimed. The row now defends its own boundary on two mutually contradicting grounds.

primary_reviews.rationale: The lexical binding this row rests on survives testing, and I can put a number on it: a skeleton sweep of the hiphil stem written העיר returns exactly 2 occurrences across the whole book, at oshb:Ezra.1.1 and oshb:Ezra.1.5, both governing the object phrase 'spirit'. So the stirring collocation genuinely is confined to Cyrus and to the returning heads of households, and the row's claim that one movement binds them is not overstated — it is the strongest thing in the row. Two lesser matters do not hold up. The syntactic label attached to the phrase governed by lamed in Ezra.1.5 is inaccurate, since purpose in that verse is carried by the following infinitives construct לַעֲל֣וֹת לִבְנ֔וֹת rather than by the lamed phrase. More consequentially, the clause type the row uses to justify closing before Ezra.1.7 is the same clause type it declares insufficient at Ezra.1.6, and that asymmetry is not defended.

challenges.claim: The row closes before Ezra.1.7 because Cyrus 'shifts subject and topic outright', while its rejected alternative refuses Ezra.1.6 a boundary because 'the text does not re-frame with its own opener'. Both verses carry an identical construction: וְכָל סְבִיבֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ חִזְּק֣וּ at oshb:Ezra.1.6 is waw plus fronted nominal subject plus piel perfect third masculine plural, and וְהַמֶּ֣לֶךְ כּ֔וֹרֶשׁ הוֹצִ֖יא at oshb:Ezra.1.7 is waw plus fronted nominal subject plus hiphil perfect third masculine singular. Each is disjunctive against the wayyiqtol that opens oshb:Ezra.1.5. Tier 1 on both sides, from morphology and clause order. The assertion that 1:6 supplies no opener of its own is therefore not true of the Hebrew, and the criterion is being applied unevenly to two adjacent seams.
challenges.suggested_action: Separate the two seams on grounds the clause type cannot supply — Ezra.1.6 keeps the donative semantics and the beneficiary field of Ezra.1.5, whereas Ezra.1.7 introduces a new agent and a new class of object — or strike the 'no opener' phrasing from the rejected alternative.

challenges.claim: The phrase לְכֹ֨ל הֵעִ֤יר הָאֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת רוּח֔וֹ at oshb:Ezra.1.5 is called a 'motive clause'. Its syntax is an asyndetic relative governed by the lamed quantifier, extending the subject set of the opening wayyiqtol rather than stating a cause; there is no causal conjunction and no causal infinitive. Purpose in the verse belongs to לַעֲל֣וֹת לִבְנ֔וֹת , the infinitive pair dependent on that same verb. Tier 1, from morphology.
challenges.suggested_action: Relabel it as a specifying relative apposed to the subject, and cite the infinitive pair if a purpose element is wanted in the argument.

primary_reviews.rationale: The wayyiqtol opener at 1:5 and the stirred-spirit echo back to 1:1 are both real and byte-confirmed, and the row rightly treats the neighbors' contribution in 1:6 as part of the same mobilization wave rather than a new unit; the pivot to Cyrus's own vessel-giving at 1:7 is a genuine actor-and-action change that correctly closes the row. But the stated reason for why 1:6 is not its own row does not survive the same syntactic test applied one verse later -- see the challenge below.

challenges.claim: The rationale rejects splitting 1:5 from 1:6 by asserting 1:6 'does not re-frame with its own opener,' but 1:6 opens with the same construction type as the very verse that DOES open the next row: fronted subject plus qatal, not a wayyiqtol continuation. 1:6 opens וְכָל סְבִיבֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ חִזְּק֣וּ (byte-sliced from verse_map_oshb.json) and 1:7 -- accepted by M8-Ezra-003 as a fresh-unit opener -- opens וְהַמֶּ֣לֶךְ כּ֔וֹרֶשׁ הוֹצִ֖יא (also byte-sliced), the identical disjunctive-subject-plus-qatal pattern set against the wayyiqtol chain (1:5's וַיָּק֜וּמוּ, 1:8's וַיּֽוֹצִיאֵ֗ם). Since the same syntactic form occurs at both an accepted and a rejected boundary, opener-presence cannot be the real differentiator; the genuine warrant is content-level continuity (same donor-action class, widened participant set) versus 1:7's different actor and different action-class, and the rationale should say so rather than leaning on a syntactic test the next verse contradicts.
challenges.suggested_action: Reword the rejected-alternative sentence to ground the 1:5|1:6 non-boundary call in actor/action-class continuity rather than 'its own opener,' since that phrasing is falsified by 1:7's identical construction at a boundary the campaign does accept.

primary_reviews.rationale: v1 adds a new differentiation warrant: 'both 1:5 and 1:6 sharing the disjunctive waw-fronted-subject-qatal clause type against the wayyiqtol chain.' Ezra.1.5 in fact opens וַיָּק֜וּמוּ רָאשֵׁ֣י הָאָב֗וֹת -- a verb-initial wayyiqtol clause (byte-confirmed in verse_map_oshb.json), not a subject-fronted qatal clause -- and this same row's own opening sentence already calls it 'a wayyiqtol opener.' The claim also contradicts sibling row M8-Ezra-001's v1, which relies on 'Ezra.1.5's wayyiqtol, וַיָּק֜וּמוּ' as the cutoff for the preceding volitive chain. Only Ezra.1.6 (וְכָל סְבִיבֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ חִזְּק֣וּ, subject before qatal) and Ezra.1.7 (וְהַמֶּ֣לֶךְ כּ֔וֹרֶשׁ הוֹצִ֖יא) actually share the disjunctive waw-subject-qatal pattern the new warrant describes; 1:5 does not, so the seam-differentiation argument rests on a misdescribed clause and disagrees with the neighboring row's repaired analysis of the same verse.

primary_reviews.rationale: The opening edge is fine and the verb description is accurate — Ezra.1.7 fronts its subject before a perfect, then the narration does run as a chain, with a wayyiqtol closing verse 7 and two more opening and closing verse 8. Where the row is exposed is its closing edge, which hangs on a single formula at Ezra.1.9 doing unit-opening work. I swept that formula and it does not behave that way consistently in this book: two of its five genuine attestations open a subsection inside a larger register, and one of those is not even clause-initial in its verse. On top of that, the narrative thread the row closes at Ezra.1.8 is resumed at Ezra.1.11 with the same participant, which means the inventory sits bracketed inside the transfer report rather than standing beside it. Under the strategy's inset test that pattern argues for holding Ezra.1.7 through Ezra.1.11 together, because the resumption that would license detaching the list falls inside the next row instead of after the inset. The medium confidence carried by the row is appropriate; the seam is genuinely live.

challenges.claim: The whole close rests on וְאֵ֖לֶּה מִסְפָּרָ֑ם at oshb:Ezra.1.9 counting as a unit-opening incipit. A skeleton sweep of that opener returns 6 hits book-wide, of which five are this demonstrative: oshb:Ezra.1.9, oshb:Ezra.2.1, oshb:Ezra.2.59, oshb:Ezra.8.1 and oshb:Ezra.8.13. Two of those five open a subsection within a larger register rather than a unit: וְאֵ֗לֶּה הָֽעֹלִים֙ at oshb:Ezra.2.59 inside the chapter 2 register, and וְאֵ֣לֶּה שְׁמוֹתָ֔ם at oshb:Ezra.8.13, which follows וּמִבְּנֵ֣י אֲדֹנִיקָם֮ אַחֲרֹנִים֒ within its own verse and so is not clause-initial. The formula demonstrably operates below unit level in this book and cannot carry the seam alone. Reinforcing the point, הַכֹּ֞ל הֶעֱלָ֣ה שֵׁשְׁבַּצַּ֗ר at oshb:Ezra.1.11 resumes exactly the thread left at וַֽיִּסְפְּרֵם֙ לְשֵׁשְׁבַּצַּ֔ר in oshb:Ezra.1.8, same participant and same transaction, so on the strategy's inset test the required resumption lands inside the following row rather than after the inset. For completeness on the sweep: the sixth hit is a false positive from a different language, namely the determined noun וֵֽאלָהָ֞א at oshb:Ezra.6.12, which is Aramaic and inside the 4:8-6:18 zone.
challenges.suggested_action: Either supply an additional warrant for the Ezra.1.8 to Ezra.1.9 cut that the sub-unit attestations at 2:59 and 8:13 do not undercut, or merge Ezra.1.7 through Ezra.1.11 as one transfer unit hosting the inventory as an inset.

challenges.claim: 'the incipit particle' misclassifies the word at oshb:Ezra.1.9. In וְאֵ֖לֶּה מִסְפָּרָ֑ם the opener is a demonstrative pronoun serving as fronted subject of a verbless clause whose predicate is the suffixed noun that follows it; it is not a particle. Tier 1, word class.
challenges.suggested_action: Write demonstrative pronoun, or demonstrative-fronted nominal clause, in place of particle.

primary_reviews.rationale: The fresh-subject opener at 1:7 and the run of narrative verbs into 1:8's hand-off to Sheshbazzar are accurately quoted, and oshb confirms 1:8 continues the wayyiqtol chain (וַיּֽוֹצִיאֵ֗ם) rather than breaking it, which is consistent with treating 1:7-8 as one narrative stretch. The closing argument is the strongest part of this row: 1:9's nominal incipit וְאֵ֖לֶּה מִסְפָּרָ֑ם genuinely breaks the verb chain and formally anticipates 2:1's וְאֵ֣לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֗ה, confirmed as the identical opening particle in oshb. This row also does the honest thing of naming the strategy's own coarser block-map suggestion (1:7-11 as one sub-seam) as its rejected alternative and arguing past it with a real device parallel, rather than silently overriding the strategy.

strongest_rejected_alternative narrates the pipeline's own adjudication process rather than arguing the text: 'This row holds the finer Ezra.1.7-Ezra.1.8 | Ezra.1.9-Ezra.1.11 cut on the syntactic-class switch ... -- but the coarser inset reading remains a live rival for the boss, not a settled question' names the pipeline's 'boss' adjudicator by role and frames the boundary as pending a ruling rather than as an argued position. The same field's opening clause, '...is the stronger rival than a defense resting on the incipit alone could answer,' likewise narrates the inadequacy of this row's own prior (v0) defense rather than engaging the rival reading on textual grounds.

primary_reviews.rationale: Calling Ezra.1.11 a colophon is defensible and I checked the device rather than assuming it: the summation word used there recurs as a totalling formula 7 times across the book by skeleton sweep, including at oshb:Ezra.2.42 within this same cluster, so the row has named a real recurring shape. The formal comparison it draws between the opener of Ezra.1.9 and the opener of Ezra.2.1 is also a genuine correspondence. But the grammatical name the row gives that shared device is simply the wrong category, and the forward-linkage argument it builds on shared captivity vocabulary is weaker than the prose implies once the lexeme is counted. Neither defect moves the span; both weaken the warrant, and the row's medium confidence should not rise on this reasoning as written.

challenges.claim: The device is described as 'a construct and-these opener'. Nothing in וְאֵ֖לֶּה מִסְפָּרָ֑ם at oshb:Ezra.1.9 stands in the construct state: it is a verbless clause pairing a demonstrative subject with a suffixed predicate noun. At the comparandum the row itself chooses, וְאֵ֣לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֗ה at oshb:Ezra.2.1, the construct chain is the second and third words, and the demonstrative stands outside it as clause subject. The parallel between the two openers is real; the label attached to it is a state error. Tier 1, syntax and state.
challenges.suggested_action: Rename the device — demonstrative-fronted presentative nominal clause — and retain the 1:9 to 2:1 comparison unchanged.

challenges.claim: The hand-forward argument leans on הַגּוֹלָ֔ה at oshb:Ezra.1.11 recurring at oshb:Ezra.2.1 as language that 'anticipates' the register that follows. A skeleton sweep of that lexeme returns 12 occurrences book-wide, distributed over seven different chapters. At that frequency it is ordinary Ezra diction with no discriminating force at a seam, and the row presents a bare adjacency as though it were a directional signal.
challenges.suggested_action: State it as thematic adjacency rather than anticipation, and carry the sweep count in the prose so the weight of the observation is visible to the reader.

primary_reviews.rationale: The incipit-to-incipit parallel this row leans on is real: 1:9's וְאֵ֖לֶּה and 2:1's וְאֵ֣לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֗ה share the identical opening particle, confirmed against oshb bytes. The colophon's closing vocabulary (הַגּוֹלָ֔ה, and the shared ע-ל-ה root between הֶעֱלָ֣ה and הָֽעֹלִים֙) genuinely anticipates 2:1 without merging into it -- a catchword link, not a shared unit -- and the row argues this distinction instead of merely asserting it. The rejected alternative (letting the colophon's captivity language already open the 2:1 register) is a real, well-chosen rival given how tight that vocabulary overlap is.
No second-generation defect surfaced when this row's draft and revised texts were compared side by side.

boss_ruling.reasoning: State-label error cured (verbless demonstrative clause, not construct) and the golah hand-forward claim now carries its 12-hit distribution, downgraded from diagnostic to compatible.

primary_reviews.rationale: Two checks proper to this role, and the row passes both. One: oshb:Ezra.2.1 carries a ketiv/qere pair — the unpointed נבוכדנצור standing immediately beside the pointed נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֥ר in the OSHB line — and neither quoted slice spans it, so no disclosure is owed under the strategy's ketiv/qere rule. The other: Ezra.2.2 contains a near-homograph trap: מִסְפָּ֥ר appears as a personal name inside the leader roster and מִסְפַּ֕ר אַנְשֵׁ֖י עַ֥ם יִשְׂרָאֵֽל opens with the same consonants pointed as the noun 'number'; the row quotes the noun, correctly. The span holds too — אֲשֶׁר בָּ֣אוּ עִם זְרֻבָּבֶ֗ל continues the relative chain begun in the incipit sentence at oshb:Ezra.2.1, so verse 2 cannot be severed from verse 1, and the earliest line combining a name with a figure really is בְּנֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔שׁ at oshb:Ezra.2.3, exactly as the row says. My one reservation concerns which side of the seam the counting header belongs to, and the row's silence about a tension its own wording creates.

challenges.claim: The row assigns מִסְפַּ֕ר אַנְשֵׁ֖י עַ֥ם יִשְׂרָאֵֽל at oshb:Ezra.2.2 to the incipit frame while describing it as the phrase that 'sets up the clan-by-clan count that follows' — on the row's own account it faces forward, and syntactically it is the heading of the enumeration beginning at oshb:Ezra.2.3, not a closing element of the frame. The verse's atnach falls on בַּעֲנָ֑ה , placing that heading in the second half-verse (tier 2, disjunctive accent, corroborative and not driving anything here). Whole-verse granularity may well force the assignment, but the row asserts it without acknowledging that both the syntax and the accentuation point the other way.
challenges.suggested_action: Disclose the tension and justify the assignment from the whole-verse constraint; and consider whether the strongest rival to engage is a frame ending at the atnach rather than the extension through Ezra.2.3 that the row currently rejects.

primary_reviews.rationale: 2:1's register incipit and 2:2's frame-to-entries transition are both accurately quoted, and the frame/entry distinction the row draws is real: no verse in 2:1-2 carries a numeral, while 2:3 opens the first counted line. The rejected alternative correctly names the temptation to extend through 2:3 for a worked example and explains why doing so would blur the formal line rather than sharpen it.
No second-generation defect surfaced when this row's draft and revised texts were compared side by side.

challenge_responses.note: Disclosed that the 2:2 heading phrase sits after the atnach and syntactically heads the 2:3ff enumeration; justified keeping it in this row from whole-verse granularity; named the atnach-frame rival alongside the extension-through-2:3 rival.

boss_ruling.reasoning: The mispar phrase is now placed on the register side of the frame with the incipit proper confined to 2:1-2a, matching the class-header logic used book-wide.

primary_reviews.rationale: I tested the row's negative universal exhaustively rather than by sample. Reading the first word of every verse from oshb:Ezra.2.3 through oshb:Ezra.2.35, all 33 begin with an anarthrous construct — 29 with the 'sons of' form and 4 with the 'men of' form — and the first determined absolute plural anywhere in the register is הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים at oshb:Ezra.2.36. So the claim that no entry inside this run carries a class caption of its own is true, and the closing contrast the row draws is grammatically well founded; the claim is stated in universal form without an adjacent count, which the figures just given supply. Worth recording as well: no row in this cluster invokes a paragraph marker at any seam, which is the correct discipline in a chapter where marks follow entries throughout and a single citation would be selective. The defect is narrower and lies in the distributional statement used to dismiss the alternation between the two entry forms.

challenges.claim: 'both forms recur on both sides of Ezra.2.21-Ezra.2.23' is false for one of the two forms. The row's conclusion remains reachable, but it has to come from what follows: אַנְשֵׁ֥י נְטֹפָ֖ה and אַנְשֵׁ֣י עֲנָת֔וֹת at oshb:Ezra.2.22 and oshb:Ezra.2.23, then the 'sons of' form again from oshb:Ezra.2.24 through oshb:Ezra.2.26 including בְּנֵ֤י הָרָמָה֙ , then אַנְשֵׁ֣י מִכְמָ֔ס and אַנְשֵׁ֤י בֵֽית אֵל֙ at oshb:Ezra.2.27 and oshb:Ezra.2.28, then the 'sons of' form to the end of the run at oshb:Ezra.2.35. primary_reviews.rationale: Everything in this row that can be tested morphologically checks out. הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים at oshb:Ezra.2.36 is a determined plural in the absolute state bearing atnach, standing outside the counting formula that follows it in the same verse, and the contrast the row draws with the construct-chain entries of the roll it follows is exact — I verified it against all 33 openers from oshb:Ezra.2.3 to oshb:Ezra.2.35, none of which is determined. The arithmetic is right as well: three further clans are counted at oshb:Ezra.2.37, oshb:Ezra.2.38 and oshb:Ezra.2.39 after the Jedaiah entry that shares the caption verse, and the closing quote בְּנֵ֣י חָרִ֔ם אֶ֖לֶף וְשִׁבְעָ֥ה עָשָֽׂר collates at byte tier. The close is warranted by the strongest signal available, since הַלְוִיִּ֑ם at oshb:Ezra.2.40 reproduces the row's own opening shape, determined absolute plural plus atnach, so the device that opens the unit is the device that ends it. High confidence is earned here in a way it would not be at the vessel-list seams earlier in the cluster. One matter I flag for the mesh rather than as a defect of this row: the principle asserted in its rejected alternative, that independent class captions must not be erased, is not the principle the immediately following row applies, and the two should be adjudicated together.

This is the cleanest edge pair in the cluster: 2:36 opens on an absolute-state class caption distinct in grammatical form from every construct-chain entry before it, and 2:40 repeats the device for a new class, giving both edges independent textual warrant rather than a length-based guess. The rejected alternative (merging forward through 2:42) is well-chosen, and its objection -- that doing so erases two independent captions the text itself supplies -- is exactly right, which makes it a useful foil against M8-Ezra-008's own choice to blur that same distinction one row later.

primary_reviews.rationale: The captioning device this row invokes is real, and across chapter 2 it has one consistent shape: a determined plural standing absolute before its entries and carrying atnach — הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים at oshb:Ezra.2.36, הַלְוִיִּ֑ם at oshb:Ezra.2.40, הַֽמְשֹׁרְרִ֑ים at oshb:Ezra.2.41, הַנְּתִינִ֑ים at oshb:Ezra.2.43. The gatekeepers line does not have that shape, so the trio of parallel captions the row's cohesion argument depends on is really a pair plus an entry. The row's second warrant then misdescribes the contents of the very verse whose grouping it is defending. The close at Ezra.2.43 is correctly identified and is the soundest part of the row; my objections go to why the three verses are held together, not to where the unit stops.

challenges.claim: בְּנֵ֣י הַשֹּֽׁעֲרִ֗ים at oshb:Ezra.2.42 is listed as an 'absolute-state caption' beside הַלְוִיִּ֑ם and הַֽמְשֹׁרְרִ֑ים . It is nothing of the kind: the head noun is in the construct state and the determination sits on the nomen rectum. That is the shape of an entry line, formally identical to בְּנֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔שׁ at oshb:Ezra.2.3 or בְּנֵ֤י הָרָמָה֙ at oshb:Ezra.2.26, and formally unlike the bare determined captions at oshb:Ezra.2.40, oshb:Ezra.2.41 and oshb:Ezra.2.43. Tier 1, state and syntax. Two of the row's three parallel captions are captions; the third is an entry.
challenges.suggested_action: Withdraw the three-parallel-captions warrant and rest the bloc on some other footing, or revisit where 2:42 attaches given that the caption series actually runs 2:36, 2:40, 2:41, 2:43.

challenges.claim: The justification offered for merging classes the row concedes are separately captioned is that 'each occupies a single verse with no internal entries of its own'. That premise is false of oshb:Ezra.2.42, which enumerates six sub-families — בְּנֵי שַׁלּ֤וּם בְּנֵֽי אָטֵר֙ בְּנֵי טַלְמ֣וֹן בְּנֵי עַקּ֔וּב בְּנֵ֥י חֲטִיטָ֖א בְּנֵ֣י שֹׁבָ֑י — and then closes on a summation of its own, הַכֹּ֕ל מֵאָ֖ה שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וְתִשְׁעָֽה , the same totalling device the cluster credits as a colophon at oshb:Ezra.1.11 and which a skeleton sweep puts at 7 occurrences book-wide. Once the false half of the premise is removed, what remains is 'a single verse', which is verse counting: tier-4 metadata, and barred from grounding a granularity decision.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop the false premise and the verse-count appeal; if the bloc is retained, ground it on a criterion internal to the text, and reconcile it with the preceding row's insistence that independent class captions must not be erased.

primary_reviews.rationale: The three class captions here are accurately quoted and the gatekeepers' closing total is correctly cited. But this row's own rejected alternative concedes the stronger reading without fully answering it -- see the challenge below. Given that concession sits unresolved, and given that M8-Ezra-006 and M8-Ezra-007 both treat a fresh caption as sufficient warrant to end a row, 'medium' confidence reads as generous rather than merely cautious for this particular grain choice.

challenges.claim: This row's own rejected alternative concedes that splitting Levites/singers/gatekeepers into three rows 'would be defensible on caption grounds alone' -- and that concession deserves more weight, because caption-as-boundary is precisely the rule M8-Ezra-006 and M8-Ezra-007 use to drive boundaries elsewhere in this same register: 006 closes before 2.36's absolute-state caption הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים, and 007 closes before 2.40's parallel caption הַלְוִיִּ֑ם, each treating a fresh class caption as the row-ending signal. Ezra.2.41 (הַֽמְשֹׁרְרִ֑ים) and Ezra.2.42 (בְּנֵ֣י הַשֹּֽׁעֲרִ֗ים) are exactly such captions, each opening its own class, yet M8-Ezra-008 does not apply the caption-boundary rule to its own interior. The row's stated justification -- 'consistent with how this part treats other brief captioned groups' -- names no comparandum anywhere in boundary_evidence_refs. (Weak corroboration only, single-witness: pmarks_Ezra.json records a PE break, the stronger paragraph division, following both 2.41 and 2.42, not merely a samekh -- consistent with, though never a driver for, three sub-units here.)

primary_reviews.rationale: Every Hebrew citation in this row collates at byte tier in the verse it is credited to (הַנְּתִינִ֑ים at 2:43; בְּנֵ֖י עַבְדֵ֣י שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה at 2:55; the joint total at 2:58; וְאֵ֗לֶּה הָֽעֹלִים֙ at 2:59), and 2:43-2:58 is Hebrew throughout, so no zone label is at risk. The load-bearing claim is that neither sub-list is separately totalled, and it survives inspection: 2:54 ends בְּנֵ֥י חֲטִיפָֽא and 2:57 ends בְּנֵ֥י אָמִֽי, both without a numeral, so the register withholds its own closing device until 2:58. That is what makes the 2:54|2:55 caption seam formally weaker than the two edges the row actually takes — the bloc before it does close on a numeral colophon, הַכֹּ֕ל מֵאָ֖ה שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וְתִשְׁעָֽה at 2:42, so the row is not applying one criterion at 2:58 and a different one at 2:42. Weak corroboration, disclosed in full and driving nothing: WLC single-witness marks stand after 2:42 (PE) and after 2:58 (SAMEKH), and no mark at all falls inside 2:43-2:57 (0 of 15 verses); this register's marking is uneven (38 of 39 verses in 2:2-2:40 carry a mark against 7 of 30 in 2:41-2:70), so the silence across 2:43-2:57 is reported as tier-3 context only and its absence is not counted against anything. No original-language defect found.

The joint colophon is the whole case here. Two captions look at first glance like two rosters, but כָּ֨ל הַנְּתִינִ֔ים וּבְנֵ֖י עַבְדֵ֣י שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה שְׁלֹ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת תִּשְׁעִ֥ים וּשְׁנָֽיִם refuses to total them separately -- one figure (392) for both classes together, exactly as argued. Set against the earlier priests/Levites/singers/gatekeepers captions (2:36, 2:40-42), each of which is treated as its own row precisely because each carries its OWN total, this pairing's shared colophon is a genuinely distinguishing feature, not just an assertion. The edges hold: 2:42's gatekeeper total closes cleanly before 2:43, and 2:59's fresh incipit is a different device altogether (place-names, not a clan-name caption) opening a differently-typed unit.

primary_reviews.rationale: Byte collation is clean on all seven Hebrew runs, and the incipit family the row invokes checks out once the sweep is actually run: skeleton ואלה returns 6 verses (1:9, 2:1, 2:59, 6:12, 8:1, 8:13), of which 6:12 is a substring artefact (the Aramaic וֵֽאלָהָ֞א), leaving 5 genuine ואלה tokens — and all 5 head verbless presentative clauses. Inside this writer part the form occurs only at 1:9, 2:1 and 2:59, so the row's assertion about what ואלה does 'elsewhere in this part' is true; it simply arrived without the count. The unit's inner logic — one problem stated at 2:59, extended to a priestly case at 2:61 by the partitive וּמִבְּנֵי֙ הַכֹּ֣הֲנִ֔ים rather than by a class caption, and resolved for both by the governor's ruling at 2:63 — is sound, and the aggregate formula at 2:64 is a real register change. What is not sound is the treatment of the rival split, and two of the row's grammatical descriptions need repair.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative answers a weaker rival than the one the text supplies. The strongest case for splitting 2:59-2:60 from 2:61-2:63 is not that וּמִבְּנֵי֙ is a fresh incipit — it plainly is not — but that 2:60 closes with a numeral, שֵׁ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת חֲמִשִּׁ֥ים וּשְׁנָֽיִם, which is this register's own list-closing device and is precisely the criterion the immediately preceding decision (M8-Ezra-009) uses to argue that 2:43-2:57 may not be cut: there the withholding of a numeral binds the sub-lists, here the presence of one is passed over in silence. Tier-3 weak corroboration, single-witness, never a driver, disclosed in full: a SAMEKH follows 2:60 and it is the only mark anywhere in 2:59-2:63 (1 of 5 verses); it is not a per-entry artefact, because the dense entry-marking of 2:2-2:40 (38 of 39 verses) has already lapsed by this point in the chapter (2:41-2:70: 7 of 30 verses). The marker alone would be insufficient evidence; the numeral colophon is the tier-1 leg.

challenges.claim: 'a determined-state class' applies Aramaic state terminology to a Hebrew form. Ezra 2:59 is Hebrew (the zones are 4:8-6:18 and 7:12-26), and the comparandum the phrase points back at, הַנְּתִינִ֑ים at 2:43, is definite by the article הַ, not by the emphatic ־א ending that 'determined state' names in the Aramaic blocks. This is the mirror image of the defect the campaign forbids inside the zones, and the suite cannot see it: check_language_zones.py flags just the literal tokens 'Hebrew', 'Aramaic' and 'Syrian' within 100 characters of a ref, so a mislabelled state category passes it silently.
challenges.suggested_action: Replace 'determined-state class' with 'articular (definite) class noun', and reserve 'determined state' for forms inside 4:8-6:18 / 7:12-26.

challenges.claim: The criterion named for 2:62 is under-determined. The row rests the anaphora reading on the missing conjunction — אֵ֗לֶּה without the vav of וְאֵ֗לֶּה — but in-book that contrast has only two data points and does no independent work. The contrast that does the work is clause type: all 5 genuine ואלה tokens in Ezra (1:9, 2:1, 2:59, 8:1, 8:13; sweep skeleton ואלה = 6 hits, one of them the Aramaic וֵֽאלָהָ֞א of 6:12) head verbless presentative clauses, whereas 2:62 reads אֵ֗לֶּה בִּקְשׁ֧וּ כְתָבָ֛ם, a demonstrative subject governing a finite qatal — a clause, not a heading.
challenges.suggested_action: Rest the non-incipit reading of 2:62 on the finite-verb clause type with the 5-token sweep cited adjacently, keeping the vav observation as secondary.

primary_reviews.rationale: The vav-less אֵ֗לֶּה at 2:62 against the vav-bearing וְאֵ֗לֶּה at 2:59 is a real, checkable distinction and it does the row's central work: 2:62 looks back anaphorically rather than opening anything new, so the priests of 2:61-63 stay inside the same unresolved-status unit as the laity of 2:59-60 rather than forming their own row. That argument is sound as far as it goes. But the row measures 2:61's וּמִבְּנֵי֙ הַכֹּ֣הֲנִ֔ים against only one incipit family -- 2:59's list-restart form -- and never against the OTHER device this same chapter already treats as row-opening: the bare class-caption (הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים at 2:36, and its counterparts at 2:40-43). 2:61 shares its head noun with 2:36's own priestly caption. The row's real defense is the added vav-conjunction plus מִן-partitive framing, which it gestures at ('conjunctive opener') but never states as the operative rule against the closer rival.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative tests 2:61's וּמִבְּנֵי֙ הַכֹּ֣הֲנִ֔ים only against the list-restart incipit וְאֵ֗לֶּה (2:59) and finds it lacking that form, but never weighs it against the other incipit family this chapter already grants independent row-opening force: bare/construct class-name captions -- הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים (2:36, priests) and its parallels at 2:40, 2:41, 2:42, 2:43 -- none of which carries a vav-prefixed restart marker either, yet each opens its own row per the block map. 2:61 shares its head noun with 2:36's own caption; the row leans on the added vav-conjunction and מִן-partitive to distinguish 2:61 from a header but never states this as the operative rule, nor tests 2:61 against the header family directly.
challenges.suggested_action: Strengthen the rejected-alternative paragraph to name the class-header device family (2:36/40/41/42/43) as the closer rival, and state explicitly why the vav-conjunction plus מִן-partitive in 2:61 marks it as continuation rather than a fresh caption of that same type.

challenges.claim: The repair installs a book-wide exclusivity claim -- 'the verbless presentative pattern that ACTUALLY opens fresh list units in this book' -- resting on a hand-enumerated list with no adjacent sweep count. sweep.py --skel over the consonantal skeleton returns 6 refs, one of which is a skeleton false positive where the same consonants spell the noun for 'God' rather than the demonstrative. primary_reviews.rationale: Both edges hold on original-language grounds. At 2:64 כָּל הַקָּהָ֖ל כְּאֶחָ֑ד aggregates where everything before it enumerated, and at 2:68 the fronted prepositional phrase וּמֵרָאשֵׁי֙ הָֽאָב֔וֹת with the infinitive-construct temporal בְּבוֹאָ֕ם restarts narration; all five Hebrew runs collate at byte tier. The row has also identified something real about the interior of the block — the heads in 2:65-2:67 (עַבְדֵיהֶ֤ם, סוּסֵיהֶ֕ם, פִּרְדֵיהֶ֕ם, גְּמַ֨לֵּיהֶ֔ם) carry a 3mp pronominal suffix instead of a construct chain built on a clan or place name, and no entry head earlier in the chapter does that. The problem is that the row names the wrong feature and states it as an exclusivity without a count. One further observation, not a challenge: the Hebrew slice at 2:65 runs one word past its English anchor and ends on אֵ֔לֶּה, which WEB renders not at all; the English given is verbatim WEB, so fidelity is intact, but the pairing should not be read as word-for-word coverage.

challenges.claim: 'This asyndetic pattern is shared by no clan or class entry earlier in the chapter' is false as worded, and it is an exclusivity claim carrying no sweep count. Asyndeton is this register's default, not a distinguishing mark of 2:64-2:67: every entry verse in 2:3-2:35 opens without a conjunction (33 of 33, all headed by בְּנֵי or by אַנְשֵׁ֥י of 2:22 — e.g. 2:3 בְּנֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔שׁ), and the class captions at 2:36, 2:40, 2:41 and 2:43 are equally unconjoined. The feature that actually is confined to this block is the one the row names in the same breath and then abandons — a possessive head with a 3mp suffix in place of a construct chain with a clan or place name (סוּסֵיהֶ֕ם, פִּרְדֵיהֶ֕ם, גְּמַ֨לֵּיהֶ֔ם). The Tier-0 suite could not catch it: check_universals.py keys on a fixed lexicon of ten exclusivity words, and the phrasing 'shared by no ... entry' matches none of them, so the gate passed the row.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop 'asyndetic', restate the distinguishing feature as the suffixed possessive head replacing the construct chain, and attach an adjacent count for whatever exclusivity is retained.

primary_reviews.rationale: Two separate observations here, both genuine. First, the structural claim that כָּל הַקָּהָ֖ל כְּאֶחָ֑ד through 2:67's noun-plus-figure lines lack any construct-chain clan header, unlike every earlier entry in the chapter, checks out -- I read every entry from 2:2 through 2:63 in oshb and each one opens with a clan or place construct-chain header. That is exactly the kind of claim the toolkit's universal-claim rule wants an adjacent count for, and the row supplies none. Second, and more substantively: the row uses that same asyndetic-onset test to mark 2:64-67 off as one unit, but never turns the test on its own interior. סוּסֵיהֶ֕ם at 2:66 has no conjunction at all and shares no vocabulary with 2:64's כָּל הַקָּהָ֖ל כְּאֶחָ֑ד or 2:65's מִ֠לְּבַד עַבְדֵיהֶ֤ם וְאַמְהֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ אֵ֔לֶּה -- arguably a sharper break than the one separating this row from 2:59-63. The closing argument (2:68's new subject and temporal clause) is solid and the outer edges are fine; it is the interior granularity that goes unaddressed.

challenges.claim: The claim that the asyndetic bare-noun-plus-figure pattern of 2:65-67 'is shared by no clan or class entry earlier in the chapter' is a universal (none) claim spanning roughly thirty preceding list entries (2:2-2:63), but no adjacent count is cited to substantiate it, as the toolkit's universal-claim rule requires. Checking every entry from 2:2 through 2:63 against oshb bytes independently, the claim holds -- each opens with a construct-chain clan or place header, with 2:65's מִ֠לְּבַד עַבְדֵיהֶ֤ם וְאַמְהֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ אֵ֔לֶּה and 2:66-67's bare noun-plus-suffix forms the only exceptions -- but the row itself supplies no count, and the phrasing ('shared by no... earlier in the chapter') differs enough from only/always/never/unique/first/sole/densest that an automated universal-claim check keyed to those terms could miss it.
challenges.suggested_action: Add the entry count the claim was checked against (approx. 30 preceding class/clan entries, 2:2-2:63), consistent with the sweep-citation rule for universal claims.

challenges.claim: The row's own diagnostic for what marks 2:64-67 off as one distinct unit -- an asyndetic, construct-chain-free noun-plus-figure form unlike anything preceding it -- is not applied to its own interior. סוּסֵיהֶ֕ם ('their horses') at 2:66 opens with no conjunction and shares no vocabulary with 2:64's כָּל הַקָּהָ֖ל כְּאֶחָ֑ד or 2:65's מִ֠לְּבַד עַבְדֵיהֶ֤ם וְאַמְהֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ אֵ֔לֶּה -- a sharper asyndetic jump than anything within 2:64-65 itself, moving from a people-census (assembly, servants, singers) to a property-census (horses, mules, camels, donkeys) with zero transitional marking. The row treats 2:64-67 as one aggregate-summary block by genre resemblance but does not address why this internal, unmarked topic-and-vocabulary break is less boundary-relevant than the break the row itself uses to separate 2:64ff from 2:59-63.
challenges.suggested_action: Add a sentence to the boundary_rationale addressing why the people/livestock shift at 2:66 stays interior to one unit -- e.g., argue that כָּל הַקָּהָ֖ל כְּאֶחָ֑ד functions as a header governing the whole census report through 2:67, not merely the assembly count -- rather than leaving the finer split unaddressed.

primary_reviews.rationale: The inclusio this row turns on is verifiable and narrow. Sweeps put אִ֥ישׁ לְעִירֽוֹ at 2:1 alone (skeleton לעירו, 1 book-wide) and בְּעָרֵיהֶֽם at 2:70 alone (skeleton בעריהם, 1 book-wide), so the two settlement notices that frame the register are each unique forms sharing the root עיר; the row claims the second 'answers' the first rather than repeats it, which is the accurate description of a singular-plus-suffix against a plural-plus-suffix. All six Hebrew runs collate at byte tier. I pressed two things. One: whether 2:70 really terminates the settlement motif — it does not lexically — 3:1 has בֶּעָרִ֑ים — but there the phrase sits in a circumstantial clause subordinated under a fresh time-frame opener, presupposing the settled state rather than continuing the colophon, so the edge is unaffected and the row's framing survives. Two: whether 2:70 should stand apart as its own colophon row — the only thing pointing that way is tier-3 (a doubled SAMEKH+SAMEKH after 2:69, WLC single-witness, in a chapter whose marking is uneven — 45 of 70 verses marked, 38 of 39 in 2:2-2:40 against 7 of 30 in 2:41-2:70), and marker-only evidence is insufficient either way; 2:70 opens with the continuation wayyiqtol וַיֵּשְׁב֣וּ and introduces no frame, so no tier-1 leg exists for the split and I decline to raise it. A PE after 2:67 sits at the row's opening edge as weak single-witness corroboration, nothing more.

This is a clean row. וּמֵרָאשֵׁי֙ הָֽאָב֔וֹת בְּבוֹאָ֕ם genuinely restarts narration -- new subject, temporal clause, verb of motion -- against 2:67's static livestock figure. The inclusio claim linking 2:70's closing וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּעָרֵיהֶֽם back to 2:1's אִ֥ישׁ לְעִירֽוֹ is not a verbatim echo -- singular idiom against plural fulfillment -- but sharing the root 'city' as the register's opening and closing key-term is a legitimate, checkable instance of the inclusio device the matrix already lists as tier-1, and both ends were confirmed against oshb. The rejected alternative (folding this into the 2:64-67 totals block) is the right rival to name; nothing stronger presents itself, since 2:68's narrative restart is a hard edge.

primary_reviews.rationale: The opening warrant is the strongest kind available here and it is correctly demonstrated: וַיִּגַּע֙ הַחֹ֣דֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י with the assembly formula וַיֵּאָסְפ֥וּ הָעָ֛ם כְּאִ֥ישׁ אֶחָ֖ד, both byte-exact, and the English quoted for 3:1 is verbatim WEB. The mark handling is accurate and properly downgraded — pmarks gives SAMEKH after 2:70 and SAMEKH+SAMEKH after 3:1, the double is disclosed, single-witness is stated, and the row says outright that these drive nothing; nor is this selective disclosure, since the mark cited at 2:70 follows the register's settlement colophon rather than a list entry, and no mark at all falls inside 3:2-3:6. The close at 3:6 is well chosen: וְהֵיכַ֥ל יְהוָ֖ה לֹ֥א יֻסָּֽד withholds a phrase that recurs exactly once more in the book (skeleton היכל יהוה = 2 verses, 3:6 and 3:10). What fails is the verb-chain description used to defeat the 3:4 split, and one statement about where the withheld item is supplied.

challenges.claim: 'continue in one unbroken 3rd-plural chain' is falsified at the head of the stretch it describes and blurred inside it. The claimed span begins at 3:2, which opens וַיָּקָם֩ יֵשׁ֨וּעַ בֶּן יֽוֹצָדָ֜ק — a 3ms wayyiqtol taking a compound subject — with the plural chain beginning at וַיִּבְנ֕וּ later in the same verse. Within 3:3 the text carries a number-divergent ketiv/qere at exactly the verb in question, ויעל (3ms) beside וַיַּעֲל֨וּ (3mp), which strategy §4 requires be disclosed when the stretch is argued from; and 3:5 has no finite verb at all, continuing 3:4 nominally. The unit's integrity is not thereby overturned — the wayyiqtol chain does run continuously and no new subject enters at 3:4 — but the description as given is an original-language claim that the text does not support.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate as a continuous narrative wayyiqtol chain under one compound subject (3ms head at 3:2, plural continuation), disclose the 3:3 ketiv/qere, and mirror oshb:Ezra.3.2 and oshb:Ezra.3.3 into boundary_evidence_refs since the claim is made about those verses.

challenges.claim: 'a proleptic notice that withholds the very thing the next unit supplies' misplaces the payoff. The unit immediately following is 3:7-3:9, which supplies funding, materials, a date and personnel but not the root יסד anywhere in it; the withheld item returns at 3:10 (וְיִסְּד֥וּ), one row further on — which is where the adjacent decision M8-Ezra-015 rightly locates the resumption. Sweeps put the root at 5 verses book-wide across its two spellings — skeleton יסד 4 hits (3:6, 3:10, 3:12, 7:9) plus skeleton הוסד 1 hit (3:11) — and none of them falls in 3:7-3:9; the phrase היכל יהוה likewise pairs 3:6 with 3:10 and no other verse (sweep: 2 hits).
challenges.suggested_action: Name 3:10 as the verse that supplies the withheld foundation notice, rather than 'the next unit'.

primary_reviews.rationale: 3:1's dated onset plus the וַיֵּאָסְפ֥וּ הָעָ֛ם כְּאִ֥ישׁ אֶחָ֖ד assembly is one of the matrix's own byte-verified tier-1 specimens, so the opening edge is about as strong as this book gets. The interior claim -- that 3:2-3 (altar) and 3:4-5 (festal calendar) run in one unbroken 3rd-plural chain -- holds up against the text: 3:4's וַֽיַּעֲשׂ֛וּ is the same wayyiqtol pattern as 3:2's וַיָּקָם֩/וַיִּבְנ֕וּ and 3:3's וַיָּכִ֤ינוּ/וַיַּעֲל֨וּ, with no new subject or frame breaking in between. The doubled SAMEKH+SAMEKH at 3:1 is disclosed correctly as tier-3, single-witness, non-driving, alongside 2:70's own SAMEKH -- proper multi-mark handling per the marker policy. The rejected alternative (splitting at 3:4) is a fair, real rival -- altar and festival are distinct liturgical acts -- but the shared subject chain and shared seventh-month frame genuinely outweigh it.

challenges.claim: The row demotes a tier-1 device without arguing the demotion. Ezra 3:8 opens וּבַשָּׁנָ֣ה הַשֵּׁנִ֗ית לְבוֹאָ֞ם ... בַּחֹ֖דֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִ֑י before reaching its verb, הֵחֵ֡לּוּ — a verse-initial waw plus ב-preposition plus time expression governing a qatal. In Ezra that construction occurs 4 times book-wide and no more: 1:1 וּבִשְׁנַ֣ת אַחַ֗ת לְכ֨וֹרֶשׁ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ פָּרַ֔ס ... הֵעִ֣יר יְהוָ֗ה; 3:8; 4:6 וּבְמַלְכוּת֙ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בִּתְחִלַּ֖ת מַלְכוּת֑וֹ כָּתְב֣וּ; 4:7 וּבִימֵ֣י אַרְתַּחְשַׁ֗שְׂתָּא כָּתַ֨ב (sweep: ובשנת 1 hit, ובשנה 1 hit, ובמלכות 1 hit, ובימי 1 hit — 4 book-wide, each verse-initial and each fronting the frame before a qatal). Era/time-frame openers are tier-1 in this campaign's evidence rules, and 3:8 adds a full participant re-specification (Zerubbabel, Jeshua, their brothers, priests, Levites, all who came from the captivity). Against that, the verse the row does open at begins with a bare wayyiqtol carrying no expressed subject, וַיִּ֨תְּנוּ — continuation morphology — and receives its unit-opening force from a topic change alone. Tier-3, weak, single-witness, disclosed in full and driving nothing: PE follows 3:7 and PE follows 3:8, both interior to the proposed span, SAMEKH follows 3:9 at its close, and no mark stands at the 3:6|3:7 opening edge — the unmarked edge is not counted against the row, and the two interior PEs are noted as corroboration for the rival, nothing stronger.
challenges.suggested_action: Either move the unit opening to 3:8 (leaving 3:7 as a materials-and-grant notice attaching backward or standing alone), or argue explicitly why 3:8's date — reckoned לְבוֹאָ֞ם from the return rather than by a regnal year — falls outside the era-opener class that the strategy's own §1 makes boundary-driving; if the latter, mirror oshb:Ezra.1.1 and oshb:Ezra.4.6 as the comparanda.

challenges.claim: 'names the overseers (Zerubbabel, Jeshua, the Levites from twenty years old)' conflates the appointers with the appointed. In 3:8 Zerubbabel and Jeshua are subjects of הֵחֵ֡לּוּ and of the following וַיַּעֲמִ֣ידוּ; the ones set לְנַצֵּ֖חַ are the Levites alone — וַיַּעֲמִ֣ידוּ אֶת הַלְוִיִּ֗ם מִבֶּ֨ן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ וָמַ֔עְלָה לְנַצֵּ֖חַ. The same verb of appointment governs 3:9's לְנַצֵּ֛חַ, so the distinction matters for how the two verses are said to continue one another.

primary_reviews.rationale: The genuinely live question here is whether 3:8's second-year/second-month notice counts as its own dated-onset device, on the same footing as the book's other tier-1 era-openers (3:1, 4:24, 7:1). I pressed on this because pmarks_Ezra.json carries a PE after both 3:7 and 3:8 -- denser marking than anywhere else in this cluster outside a genuine unit edge -- which could read as corroborating a split. But the row's actual distinction survives the pressure: every tier-1 era-opener elsewhere in the matrix pairs its date with a genuinely new action and often an expanding cast (3:1's assembly, 7:1's journey); 3:8 instead specifies WHEN the same funding/building enterprise from 3:7 formally started, with the same two named leaders already on stage since 3:2. No new verb of consequence appears until 3:10's foundation-laying. That is a real, substantive difference, not just an assertion, and it matches the strategy draft's own resolved call on this exact question.

'a verified 4-member class in this book (Ezra.1.1, Ezra.3.8, Ezra.4.6, Ezra.4.7), and every member of that class outside Ezra.3.8 is boundary-driving' is a repair-installed universal with no adjacent sweep count, and the enumeration is false. Scanning verse-initial tokens across all 280 verses for waw plus the b-preposition plus a time expression plus qatal returns at least six members: the four named, plus Ezra.8.33 וּבַיּ֣וֹם הָרְבִיעִ֡י נִשְׁקַ֣ל and Ezra.9.5 וּבְמִנְחַ֣ת הָעֶ֗רֶב קַ֚מְתִּי (the only other verse-initial waw-plus-b tokens in the book are Ezra.10.31 and Ezra.10.38, which are patronymics, not the preposition). Ezra.8.33 sits unit-interior in the 8:31-36 delivery report on the book strategy's own block map, which breaks the 'every member is boundary-driving' parity the row's escalation rests on. primary_reviews.rationale: This row's central claim is the one I could test hardest, and it holds with room to spare. A skeleton sweep of היכל יהוה returns exactly two verses book-wide, 3:6 and 3:10 — so the phrase the row calls 'the same underlying phrase' is confined to the two verses it links, and the row's hedged wording ('compare', 'underlying') does not overclaim byte identity, which would be wrong: the forms differ in accentuation (3:6 הֵיכַ֥ל יְהוָ֖ה against 3:10 הֵיכַ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה). The verbal link is stated with equal care — יֻסָּֽד at 3:6 is a passive (Pual) perfect, וְיִסְּד֥וּ at 3:10 an active Piel perfect, and the row claims no more than root-sharing. Worth adding as corroboration rather than correction: 3:10's onset is waw plus qatal, not a wayyiqtol, which is exactly the profile of a resumptive or circumstantial clause and so reinforces 'resumption, not fresh topic'. The close is secure — 4:1 brings in a new subject under a wayyiqtol — and the tier-3 picture, single-witness and non-driving, lines up without being needed: SAMEKH after 3:9 at the opening edge, SAMEKH after 3:11 interior, PE after 3:13 at the close, all disclosed together. No original-language defect found; the rejected alternative (running through 4:3) is a real rival and is answered on participant grounds.

The resumption claim is the strongest device argument in this cluster: וְיִסְּד֥וּ הַבֹּנִ֖ים אֶת הֵיכַ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה literally answers 3:6's closing וְהֵיכַ֥ל יְהוָ֖ה לֹ֥א יֻסָּֽד, sharing both the root for 'found' and the phrase 'temple of Yahweh' -- confirmed against oshb, and correctly described as a shared root rather than an identical form (the 3:6 form is passive, the 3:10 form is active), which is the right level of precision. The closing edge at 3:13 into 4:1 is equally clean: 3:13 synthesizes the weeping and shouting into one indistinguishable noise, and 4:1 introduces a wholly new cast with no scene continuity. I looked for a plausible interior split at 3:11/3:12 (song giving way to mixed weeping) but 3:13's own summary treats both reactions as one simultaneous, undifferentiated event, which argues against a split there rather than for one.

challenges.claim: The row's single formal warrant for closing at 4:3 is an original-language claim that is asserted in English and not demonstrated: 'Ezra.4.4 switches to durative participles', with boundary_evidence_refs carrying web:Ezra.4.4 and web:Ezra.4.5 and no oshb counterpart for either. The claim cannot be read off the English, where 'weakened', 'troubled' and 'hired' are all simple past. It is nevertheless true — 4:4 runs וַיְהִי֙ עַם הָאָ֔רֶץ מְרַפִּ֖ים יְדֵ֣י עַם יְהוּדָ֑ה with a second participle וּֽמְבַהֲלִ֥ים, a periphrastic durative, and 4:5 continues וְסֹכְרִ֧ים עֲלֵיהֶ֛ם יוֹעֲצִ֖ים — so the fix is quotation, not retraction. Note that the argued word at 4:4 carries a ketiv/qere, ומבלהים beside וּֽמְבַהֲלִ֥ים, which a quotation must disclose.

primary_reviews.rationale: The closing device claim is precise and checks out: 4:4's מְרַפִּ֖ים and וּֽמְבַהֲלִ֥ים are genuine Piel participles, a durative/iterative form distinct from the perfective wayyiqtol narration of the 4:1-3 exchange, and that grammatical distinction -- not just a topic change -- is what the row leans on to place the edge at 4:3/4:4. The opening edge (4:1's new-cast subject) and the quoted refusal at 4:3 both matched oshb byte-for-byte. The rejected alternative (folding 4:4-5 in as 'the full campaign') is well-chosen since it is the most natural over-read available -- a reader tracking 'opposition to the temple' as one topic could easily miss the verb-form shift the row catches.

The repair sharpens Ezra.4.4 to a 'periphrastic durative construction', which is right, but then summarises the edge in both fields as 'wayyiqtol chain giving way to durative participles'. The construction the row itself quotes opens with וַיְהִי֙ עַם הָאָ֔רֶץ -- a wayyiqtol -- followed by the participle מְרַפִּ֖ים, so the chain does not stop at 4:3|4:4; its predicate turns durative. v0's looser wording ('past narrative tense', 'different verb forms') asserted no form-class boundary that the row's own quotation contradicts.

primary_reviews.rationale: Every original-language claim in this row collates at byte tier and both edges hold, though the strongest unity argument is one the row leaves implicit. Ezra.4.4 sets up a durative frame with וַיְהִי֙ governing the participle מְרַפִּ֖ים; Ezra.4.5 then contributes no finite verb at all -- its וְסֹכְרִ֧ים is a second participle still under that same governing verb, so the pair forms one syntactic period rather than two summary sentences placed side by side. At the far edge the contrast drawn is morphologically real: Ezra.4.6 switches to a suffix-conjugation form, כָּתְב֣וּ, under a fresh dated formula. The grammatical vocabulary used matches the language of this stretch, which lies wholly before the change of script, and the ketiv/qere in Ezra.4.4 (ומבלהים וּֽמְבַהֲלִ֥ים) falls outside every quoted run, so no disclosure was owed at this row. I also put a number behind the horizon claim, which the row asserts but does not count: the four-word string מַלְכ֖וּת דָּרְיָ֥וֶשׁ מֶֽלֶךְ פָּרָֽס occurs exactly twice book-wide at byte tier (sweep: 2 -- Ezra.4.5, Ezra.4.24), so the word verbatim is exact rather than impressionistic.

The edge holds at both ends. The shift from bounded dialogue to an iterative present-participle description (מְרַפִּ֖ים) is a genuine discourse-mode change, and 4:5's temporal envelope closing at the Cyrus-to-Darius horizon gives the pair a durative frame that a single verse could not carry alone. The close at 4:6 is well-reasoned: a perfect-tense כָּתְב֣וּ notice under its own dated formula naming a different king is formally discontinuous with the participial report, and the rejected alternative correctly isolates that tense-and-formula shift as the reason an extension through 4:6 fails. The forward pointer to 4:24's echoing horizon is properly deferred to that row rather than re-litigated here.

primary_reviews.rationale: Mark handling is correct: pmarks_Ezra.json does record a SAMEKH following Ezra.4.6, the row labels it single-witness, and it is offered as weak corroboration and not as the reason for the seam, which is the right treatment for a Writings book. The two-notices reading is also better supported than the row says. Beyond the different royal names, the verbs differ in number: Ezra.4.6 has a plural כָּתְב֣וּ with no named subject, while Ezra.4.7 has a singular כָּתַ֨ב, so the notices are built differently and not merely dated differently. The row asserts that שִׂטְנָ֔ה is not continued or quoted anywhere else, which is a book-wide exclusivity claim; I checked it and it holds (sweep: 1 book-wide, with byte, accent-stripped and skeleton tiers all resolving to Ezra.4.6 alone), but the campaign requires the figure to travel with the assertion, and none is given.

primary_reviews.rationale: Zone discipline is clean here, which matters more at this verse than anywhere else in the cluster: Ezra.4.7 is handled as the Hebrew frame verse it is, no Aramaic category is imported into it even though its own subject matter is the change of language, and the letter's opening formula is correctly located at the end of Ezra.4.8 (כְּנֵֽמָא) rather than in Ezra.4.7. Both quoted runs collate byte-exact. Two narrow gaps remain. The distinctness case is built on plural correspondents, yet the verb of the verse is the singular כָּתַ֨ב and the noun following the three names carries a singular pronominal suffix and is itself a ketiv/qere pair (כנותו כְּנָוֺתָ֔יו) that the strategy flags at this very verse; neither fact is disclosed or engaged. Separately, the neighbouring one-verse row leans on a tier-3 mark while this row, whose close is followed by a PE in pmarks_Ezra.json (single-witness), says nothing about marks at all.

challenges.claim: Rationale and rejected alternative both treat Ezra.4.7 as naming plural correspondents, but the verb of that verse is singular (כָּתַ֨ב, against the plural כָּתְב֣וּ one verse earlier) and the companions-noun that follows carries a singular suffix, inside a ketiv/qere pair (כנותו כְּנָוֺתָ֔יו) named explicitly at Ezra.4.7 in the strategy. The concord is contested and the row neither discloses the pair nor states the reading it depends on. The split from Ezra.4.8 survives either construal, since the names differ regardless, so this is an evidence-quality gap and not a span error.
challenges.suggested_action: Disclose the ketiv/qere pair and state the concord reading adopted, or re-base the distinctness argument on the named individuals rather than on their number.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the most tightly argued of the cluster's three thin single-verse notices. The language-zone datum is exactly right -- 4:7 stays Hebrew even while naming the coming Aramaic ('Syrian') switch -- and the correspondent-name mismatch (Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel vs. Rehum, Shimshai) is a clean, checkable reason the verse cannot be the Rehum letter's own incipit: the letter's real address-and-כְּנֵֽמָא formula sits entirely inside 4:8, not here. v0 correctly identified Ezra.4.8's closing word as כְּנֵֽמָא ('as follows'); the repair replaces it with אִגְּרָ֥ה חֲדָ֖ה's second element and keeps the gloss 'as follows'. primary_reviews.rationale: The Aramaic substance checks out. כְּנֵֽמָא does close Ezra.4.8 and does open direct quotation; the jussive claim is accurate and correctly counted for the span, since יְדִ֨יעַ֙ לֶהֱוֵ֣א recurs at Ezra.4.13 and a sweep of the jussive gives 3 verses book-wide at byte tier (Ezra.4.12, Ezra.4.13, Ezra.5.8), only the first two of which fall inside Ezra.4.8-Ezra.4.16. Keeping the sender list and the copy formula inside the letter is right under the inset rule, and the reversal of address direction at Ezra.4.17 is a genuine close. Two precision problems sit in how the rival is dismissed and how the closing verse is labelled. Ezra.4.11 is not deviceless: דְּנָה֙ פַּרְשֶׁ֣גֶן אִגַּרְתָּ֔א appears in the strategy's own device matrix as a document-copy incipit, so what defeats a separate Ezra.4.11 row is the missing resumption after it, not a missing device. And Ezra.4.16 is no petition; it is a declarative participial clause with an independent pronoun (מְהוֹדְעִ֤ין אֲנַ֨חְנָה֙), while the request this letter actually makes is Ezra.4.15's דִּ֡י יְבַקַּר֩.

challenges.claim: The rival is turned aside on the ground that no tier-1 frame isolates the sender list or the copy formula, but Ezra.4.11 opens with דְּנָה֙ פַּרְשֶׁ֣גֶן אִגַּרְתָּ֔א, which the device matrix lists as a tier-1 document-copy incipit. The reason the rival really fails is the inset rule's double-frame requirement: an incipit with no resumption after it does not license a split. As written the dismissal reads as denying that the device is there. A single-witness PE also follows Ezra.4.11 in pmarks_Ezra.json, sitting exactly where the rival would put its seam; tier-3 can drive nothing, so this is noted purely for disclosure, but it should not go unmentioned while the rival is described as having nothing behind it.
challenges.suggested_action: Rest the dismissal on the absent resumption rather than on an absent frame, and disclose the single-witness PE following Ezra.4.11 while stating it cannot drive a boundary.

challenges.claim: Ezra.4.16 is described as a closing petition, but מְהוֹדְעִ֤ין אֲנַ֨חְנָה֙ is a declarative participial clause with an independent pronoun: the writers informing the king, not asking him for anything. The request sits in Ezra.4.15 (דִּ֡י יְבַקַּר֩). The close-edge signal available and unused is the knowledge-root chain running יְדִ֨יעַ֙ לֶהֱוֵ֣א (Ezra.4.12, repeated at Ezra.4.13), וְהוֹדַ֥עְנָא (Ezra.4.14) and מְהוֹדְעִ֤ין אֲנַ֨חְנָה֙ (Ezra.4.16), which brackets the body of the letter and warrants the close far better than the petition label does.
challenges.suggested_action: Relabel Ezra.4.16 as a declarative closing statement and argue the close from the knowledge-root bracket instead of from a petition located in Ezra.4.15.

primary_reviews.rationale: The inset-rule application is textbook: the co-senders list and the internal 'copy of the letter' formula (4:11) carry no double frame of their own and correctly travel with the address-and-incipit verse rather than forming separate rows. The jussive claim is exact rather than merely asserted once and assumed to recur: לֶהֱוֵ֣א genuinely opens both 4:12 and 4:13 in source. The 4:16/4:17 edge is unambiguous (petition verb to royal reply), and 'high' confidence is earned by the density of independently checkable tier-1 signals rather than resting on any single one.

primary_reviews.rationale: As far as it goes the Aramaic reading is sound. פִּתְגָמָ֞א שְׁלַ֣ח מַלְכָּ֗א does reverse the direction of address, שְׁלָ֖ם is an unmodified one-word greeting, and the decree-verb claim understates itself: לְבַטָּלָ֖א is the earliest occurrence of that root in the book (sweep, skeleton tier: 5 book-wide -- Ezra.4.21, Ezra.4.23, Ezra.4.24, Ezra.5.5, Ezra.6.8), so Ezra.4.23 and Ezra.4.24 are indeed picking it up rather than sharing it with earlier material. The span itself is right under the inset rule. What is uneven is the criterion. Ezra.4.23 is excluded because the royal voice disappears there, yet this row's own opening verse is third-person narration about the king; the king does not speak in his own person before Ezra.4.18, whose קָדָמָֽי carries a 1cs suffix. The frame verse does belong with its rescript, but that is the inset rule speaking, not the voice test invoked -- and the frame element that would have made the point, the verse-final וּכְעֶֽת, goes unquoted.

challenges.claim: The exclusion test and the inclusion practice do not match. Ezra.4.23 is kept out for dropping the royal voice in favour of third-person narration, but Ezra.4.17 is third-person narration too (פִּתְגָמָ֞א שְׁלַ֣ח מַלְכָּ֗א); the king speaks in his own person from Ezra.4.18 onward (קָדָמָֽי, 1cs). Applied evenly, the stated criterion would cut Ezra.4.17 from this row. The span is nonetheless correct, because the inset rule keeps a letter's frame verse with its letter -- but the row does not invoke that rule, and it stops its description of the frame at שְׁלָ֖ם, omitting the verse-final וּכְעֶֽת, the epistolary transition that actually hands off from address to rescript body (sweep, skeleton tier: 1 book-wide for this spelling, at Ezra.4.17; the fuller spelling gives 3 -- Ezra.4.10, Ezra.4.11, Ezra.7.12).
challenges.suggested_action: Re-warrant the opening edge on the letter-frame rule plus the transition formula closing Ezra.4.17, and reserve the voice test for the closing edge where it does hold.

But the row's own interior coverage is incomplete: Ezra.4.20, part of the same search-and-precedent beat the row summarizes only as '(Ezra.4.19),' never appears in the prose or in boundary_evidence_refs, leaving one interior verse of the six-verse span entirely unargued.

primary_reviews.rationale: The opening edge is well made: narration does resume in the third person after a stretch of royal command, and the root shared with Ezra.4.21 is genuine (וּבַטִּ֥לוּ הִמּ֖וֹ against לְבַטָּלָ֖א). The closing edge is where this row is thin, and its supporting count does not say what it is asked to say. Inspecting the tokens one by one, the form at Ezra.5.5 is וֶאֱדַ֛יִן, carrying the conjunction that the campaign's counts were corrected to keep visible, and the second token in Ezra.5.16 is וּמִן אֱדַ֧יִן, a prepositional phrase meaning from that time rather than a clause opener at all. Bare clause-initial tokens therefore number 6 in 6 verses (Ezra.4.9, Ezra.4.23, Ezra.5.4, Ezra.5.9, Ezra.5.16 opening token, Ezra.6.13), not 8 in 7. This row's own opener is likewise not the bare particle but the compound temporal sequence אֱדַ֗יִן מִן דִּ֞י, which further blurs the form contrast it is being asked to carry.

challenges.claim: The figure of 8 tokens across 7 verses is presented as the count of this bare opener, but two of the eight are neither bare nor openers. Ezra.5.5 reads וֶאֱדַ֛יִן with a prefixed conjunction, and the second token of Ezra.5.16 is וּמִן אֱדַ֧יִן, governed by a preposition inside the clause. Token-by-token inspection of the accent-stripped hit list (7 verses: Ezra.4.9, Ezra.4.23, Ezra.5.4, Ezra.5.5, Ezra.5.9, Ezra.5.16 twice, Ezra.6.13) yields 6 bare clause-initial tokens in 6 verses. The 8/7 figure is a lexeme count, and using it as an opener count inflates the very class the row contrasts against the rarer particle.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate the figure as a lexeme count and give the bare-opener count separately (6 tokens in 6 verses), excluding the prefixed form at Ezra.5.5 and the prepositional token at Ezra.5.16.

challenges.claim: The split from Ezra.4.24 rests on nothing but a form contrast the row itself calls mixed-function, and its own opener is the compound אֱדַ֗יִן מִן דִּ֞י rather than the bare form that contrast assumes. Stronger signals sit unargued across the two verses: Ezra.4.23 has animate human agents with plural suffix-conjugation verbs (אֲזַ֨לוּ ... וּבַטִּ֥לוּ הִמּ֖וֹ), whereas Ezra.4.24 moves to an inanimate subject (עֲבִידַ֣ת בֵּית אֱלָהָ֔א) with feminine singular agreement and the durative וַהֲוָת֙ בָּֽטְלָ֔א spanning years. A single-witness SAMEKH also follows Ezra.4.23 in pmarks_Ezra.json; tier-3 corroborates nothing on its own and is mentioned so that the disclosure stays complete.
challenges.suggested_action: Re-warrant the closing edge on the subject and aspect shift between the two verses, and demote the particle contrast to supporting material.

primary_reviews.rationale: The real driver at this seam is the person shift (royal 1st/2nd-person command to 3rd-person narration), and it is independent of the bare אֱדַ֗יִן discussion, which the row uses correctly only to differentiate 4:23 from 4:24's rarer בֵּאדַ֗יִן -- not to carry the 4:22/4:23 boundary itself. Both sweep counts check out exactly against source, including the double occurrence at 5:16.

primary_reviews.rationale: The resumptive-repetition core is the best-evidenced argument in this cluster and it verifies exactly: the four-word royal horizon מַלְכ֖וּת דָּרְיָ֥וֶשׁ מֶֽלֶךְ פָּרָֽס occurs twice book-wide at byte tier (sweep: 2 -- Ezra.4.5 and Ezra.4.24) and nowhere else, so a formula used before the change of language reappears unaltered after it. Capping confidence at medium_low with both readings acknowledged is honest, and the row is right not to follow the strategy's suggestion of a shared cessation root with Ezra.4.5, a root that verse does not contain. Three things need correcting around that core: the particle argument does not discriminate the way it is said to, the identity claim is overstated as printed and mixes two tier names, and the out-of-sequence premise is half derivable from this book at best.

challenges.claim: The claim that each of the three occurrences of בֵּאדַ֗יִן opens a fresh narrative move rather than continuing an immediately prior clause is contradicted by two of the three. Ezra.6.1 (בֵּאדַ֛יִן ... שָׂ֣ם טְעֵ֑ם) is Darius acting on the request that ends the verse immediately before it, web:Ezra.5.17. And Ezra.5.2's בֵּאדַ֡יִן is read inside this same cluster as a connector binding the building resumption to the prophetic word of Ezra.5.1 as one continuous cause-and-effect beat. A particle that does both cannot by itself decide whether Ezra.4.24 continues Ezra.4.23, which is exactly the rival being rejected.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop the fresh-move generalisation or restate it as a tendency with the two counterexamples disclosed, and let the repeated royal-horizon formula carry the detachment argument on its own.

challenges.claim: The phrase byte-identical (accent tier) mixes two rungs of the collation ladder, on which accent-stripped is a weaker, mention-grade tier than byte. More importantly the two strings as printed are not identical at any tier: collating Ezra.4.24's לְמַלְכ֖וּת דָּרְיָ֥וֶשׁ מֶֽלֶךְ פָּרָֽס against Ezra.4.5 returns tier none, because of the prefixed preposition. What is byte-identical is the four-word substring מַלְכ֖וּת דָּרְיָ֥וֶשׁ מֶֽלֶךְ פָּרָֽס, which sweeps to exactly 2 verses book-wide at byte tier (Ezra.4.5, Ezra.4.24). The finding is sound; the quoted extent and the tier label are not.
challenges.suggested_action: Quote the shared four-word substring instead of the prefixed form, label it byte tier, and attach the sweep count of 2.

challenges.claim: The statement that the dossier cites kings who reigned after Darius is half supported from inside Ezra at best. For Artaxerxes there is in-book warrant: web:Ezra.6.14 lists the decrees of Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes in that order. For Ahasuerus there is none -- the name is a hapax here (sweep, skeleton tier: 1 book-wide, at Ezra.4.6), so nothing in Ezra places his reign relative to Darius. That premise is imported from outside the text while being stated as fact.
challenges.suggested_action: Mark the Ahasuerus chronology as extratextual, or rest the out-of-sequence claim on the repeated Darius horizon together with the in-book royal order at Ezra.6.14.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the strongest-built row in the cluster on its own terms: the בֵּאדַ֗יִן sweep (exactly 3 book-wide, each opening a fresh narrative move) and the byte-identical royal-horizon tail shared with 4:5 both check out precisely against source, and the row is unusually honest that both readings have real textual support. But the strongest_rejected_alternative tests only the weaker rival -- 4:24 as 4:23's trailing clause -- and does not engage the stronger one the strategy itself flags as the live tension: that 4:24's horizon could instead be read forward, as the implicit temporal frame under which 5:1's prophetic catalyst occurs, since 5:1 supplies no era/date formula of its own.

challenges.claim: The strongest_rejected_alternative field tests only the weaker rival (4:24 as 4:23's trailing clause) and not the stronger one the strategy explicitly names as live: 4:24's closing horizon, oshb:Ezra.4.24 “עַ֚ד שְׁנַ֣ת תַּרְתֵּ֔ין לְמַלְכ֖וּת דָּרְיָ֥וֶשׁ מֶֽלֶךְ פָּרָֽס” ("until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia," web:Ezra.4.24, byte tier), is textually available to read forward as the implicit time-frame governing 5:1's prophetic catalyst and 5:2's building resumption, since oshb:Ezra.5.1's own opening וְהִתְנַבִּ֞י חַגַּ֣י... supplies no independent era/date formula of its own -- unlike every other unit-opening era-marker in the book (1:1, 3:1, 7:1, 9:1). The row's own perfect-tense verbs בְּטֵלַת֙/בָּֽטְלָ֔א ('stopped'/'was stopped,' byte tier) describe a completed cessation-state rather than opening fresh action the way those era-openers do, which IS a real textual basis for rejecting the forward-attachment rival -- but the row never makes that argument, so the rival it does reject is not demonstrably the strongest available one.
challenges.suggested_action: Either fold the forward-attachment rival into strongest_rejected_alternative with the completed-cessation-vs-fresh-action distinction as the textual reason it fails, or note the unresolved tension explicitly alongside the existing confidence cap.

primary_reviews.rationale: New rejected-alternative text asserts Ezra.5.1 “supplies no independent era formula of its own, unlike every other unit-opener in the book (1:1, 3:1, 7:1, 9:1)” -- an exclusivity claim with no adjacent sweep count. Checked against the text: Ezra.8.1 also opens with an independent regnal formula (“in the reign of Artaxerxes the king”, web:Ezra.8.1) yet is omitted; Ezra.9.1 (“when these things were done”, web:Ezra.9.1) is anaphoric to prior narrative, not an independent era formula; Ezra.3.1 (“when the seventh month had come”, web:Ezra.3.1) is a calendar-month marker, not a royal-reign formula of the same kind as 1:1/7:1. The four-item list is neither exhaustive nor uniform in kind.
