primary_reviews.rationale: Morphology and disclosure are handled well. וְהִתְנַבִּ֞י is a reflexive-stem suffix-conjugation form and is not given a label borrowed from the wrong language; all three ketiv/qere pairs across Ezra.5.1 and Ezra.5.2 are disclosed with both members quoted, and every run collates byte-exact. The closing edge is real: Ezra.5.3 opens on בֵּהּ זִמְנָא֩, a temporal frame bringing in an agent who has not appeared before. The trouble is the reason given for rejecting the rival. Continuity with Ezra.4.24 is asserted to be absent, yet the second verse of this very unit reproduces Ezra.4.24's head phrase -- בֵּית אֱלָהָ֔א דִּ֖י בִּירוּשְׁלֶ֑ם at Ezra.4.24 against בֵּ֥ית אֱלָהָ֖א דִּ֣י בִירֽוּשְׁלֶ֑ם at Ezra.5.2, a consonantal skeleton that sweeps to 3 verses book-wide (Ezra.4.24, Ezra.5.2, Ezra.5.16) -- and both verses open with the same particle followed by a suffix-conjugation verb.

challenges.claim: The rival is dismissed for having no lexical overlap with Ezra.4.24 and no shared clause type, and both halves fail at unit level. Ezra.5.2 shares five skeleton tokens with Ezra.4.24 -- the relative particle, house, God, in-Jerusalem, and the opening particle itself -- including the phrase בֵּית אֱלָהָ֔א דִּ֖י בִּירוּשְׁלֶ֑ם reproduced as בֵּ֥ית אֱלָהָ֖א דִּ֣י בִירֽוּשְׁלֶ֑ם (sweep, skeleton tier: 3 book-wide -- Ezra.4.24, Ezra.5.2, Ezra.5.16); and Ezra.4.24 and Ezra.5.2 are both particle-plus-suffix-conjugation clauses, so the clause type is shared too. Restricted to Ezra.5.1 by itself the overlap reduces to the relative particle, but the unit defended is Ezra.5.1-Ezra.5.2. The seam still stands on the change of subject and semantic domain; what fails is the ground chosen for rejecting continuity, which happens to be the ground on which the rival is strongest.
challenges.suggested_action: Reject the rival on topical and participant grounds and drop the lexical-overlap denial, or acknowledge the Ezra.5.2 repetition of Ezra.4.24 and argue that it is thematic pickup rather than clause continuation.

primary_reviews.rationale: The topic/subject-shift argument at the 4:24/5:1 seam stands on its own regardless of the temporal-frame question raised against row 023: a wholly new grammatical subject (the two named prophets) and verb stem with no lexical bridge to 4:24's administrative closing is a genuine tier-1 discontinuity in its own right. All three ketiv/qere pairs across 5:1-5:2 are disclosed and match source exactly, and the prophets-word inclusio closing the unit at 5:2 before 5:3's fresh 'at that time' frame introduces a new agent is a fair, checkable literary observation rather than an asserted one.
Comparison of the original against the repaired wording left this row without any filed finding.

challenge_responses.note: Dropped the 'no lexical overlap' claim (5:2 shares five skeleton tokens with 4:24, including a near-verbatim phrase) and re-based the rejection on topic/participant shift instead, treating the 5:2 phrase-echo as thematic pickup rather than clause continuation.

boss_ruling.reasoning: The dismissal-by-no-overlap is withdrawn: 5:2 shares the bet-elaha-di-birushlem skeleton chain (3 book-wide) with 4:24, and the rival now loses on prophetic-initiative onset rather than false non-overlap.

primary_reviews.rationale: Morphology in this row is sound where it matters most. At oshb:Ezra.5.4 «אֲמַ֣רְנָא» is a peal perfect 1cp, and the row's claim about the rendering is checkable rather than rhetorical: web:Ezra.5.4 does turn it impersonal (“They also asked for the names of the men”) while the identical string at oshb:Ezra.5.9, «כְּנֵ֖מָא אֲמַ֣רְנָא לְּהֹ֑ם», is given a plural subject at web:Ezra.5.9 (“Then we asked those elders”) — so the letter-writers' voice surfacing at 5:4 is a feature of the pointed text and not an artefact of translation. The back edge holds for the reason given: «וֶאֱדַ֛יִן יְתִיב֥וּן נִשְׁתְּוָנָ֖א» at oshb:Ezra.5.5 names the very despatch whose copy-formula opens oshb:Ezra.5.6. The front edge is where the argument as written does not carry me; see the challenge. Every quoted form in this row sits at byte tier.

challenges.claim: The particle contrast that opens this unit runs against the book's own distribution, and the front edge is the edge the rejected alternative leaves untested. «בֵּהּ זִמְנָא֩» (oshb:Ezra.5.3) is a resumptive pronoun over a determined noun — 'in it, the time' — so it synchronises the incoming scene with a time frame already established (web:Ezra.5.3 “At the same time”), and it stands exactly once in the book (sweep --skel בה זמנא: 1 book-wide, oshb:Ezra.5.3), which leaves no in-book distribution to support calling it a scene-onset formula. The form the row demotes to a 'connector', «בֵּאדַ֡יִן» at oshb:Ezra.5.2, is one of exactly 3 book-wide (sweep --skel באדין: oshb:Ezra.4.24, oshb:Ezra.5.2, oshb:Ezra.6.1), and decision M8-Ezra-027 in this same cluster grades that identical set as 'each opening a fresh narrative move'. Tier-3 is disclosed in full for this neighbourhood and settles nothing either way: pmarks_Ezra.json (single-witness, WLC) has SAMEKH after Ezra.5.1, PE after Ezra.5.2, SAMEKH after Ezra.5.3 inside the span and PE after Ezra.5.5 at the back edge — a density that discriminates between none of these candidates. The untested rival is therefore an onset at 5:2 — building resumes, inspectors arrive, one move — while the strongest_rejected_alternative argues about where the letter begins, which bears on the back edge instead.
challenges.suggested_action: Either argue the demotion of «בֵּאדַ֡יִן» explicitly against its 3-instance book-wide profile, or rest the front edge on the participant and scene change (Tattenai and Shethar-Bozenai enter, absent from 5:1-2), which carries it without the particle contrast; and put the 5:2 onset in the rejected-alternative slot.

primary_reviews.rationale: The front edge holds: Tattenai is genuinely absent from 5:1-5:2 (confirmed against oshb text), and בֵּהּ זִמְנָא֩ at 5:3 legitimately reads as a scene/participant-change opener under the tier-1 category even though it isn't itemized in the strategy's device matrix. The 5:4 אֲמַ֣רְנָא observation is genuinely productive rather than decorative: WEB's third-person smoothing ('They also asked for the names of the men') against MT's 1cp is verified, and the letter body at 5:8-9 does continue in 1cp, so the claim that 5:4 anticipates the letter's own voice-register is textually earned. The close at 5:5's providential aside handing off to 5:6's copy-formula is solid. My reservation is a device-characterization inconsistency within the cluster, flagged below.

challenges.claim: The rationale calls 5:2's בֵּאדַ֡יִן merely 'a connector' in order to set up 5:3's בֵּהּ זִמְנָא֩ as the unit's true scene-onset device. But the cluster's own M8-Ezra-027 treats בֵּאדַ֡יִן as one of only 3 book-wide discourse-openers, 'each opening a fresh narrative move' -- explicitly including this same occurrence at 5:2. The two rows in this cluster characterize the identical particle's discourse function inconsistently.
challenges.suggested_action: Align the characterization across the cluster: either concede that 5:2's בֵּאדַ֡יִן also opens a narrative move (and argue 5:3's distinctness from the co-occurring new-actor introduction of Tattenai, which is the stronger warrant already present in the row), or drop the 'connector' label.

This is distinct from the exempt “engaged, not dismissed” rival-engagement protocol, since it references the row's own prior text, not a rival interpretation.

primary_reviews.rationale: The incipit identification survives checking: in «פַּרְשֶׁ֣גֶן אִ֠גַּרְתָּא» at oshb:Ezra.5.6 the nomen rectum is in the determined state, and the string stands in 4 verses book-wide (sweep --skel פרשגן: oshb:Ezra.4.11, oshb:Ezra.4.23, oshb:Ezra.5.6, oshb:Ezra.7.11), of which 4:11 and 5:6 are the incipit uses — 'identical in kind to 4:11' is fair. The prescript close at oshb:Ezra.5.7, the petition close at oshb:Ezra.5.17 and the letter's terminus before oshb:Ezra.6.1 are all byte-exact and not in doubt. Three supporting statements do not survive: the particle sweep behind the back edge, the single-speaker premise on which the rejected alternative rests, and the scope of the '3 times' figure. In my judgement none of them moves the span — 5:6-5:17 is very probably one letter — but the row misdescribes its own evidence at three separate points.

challenges.claim: The petition-particle count is stated on a form that occurs once. The row cites «וּכְעַ֞ן» as recurring '6 times book-wide framing requests or directives' over the list 4:13, 4:14, 4:21, 5:16, 5:17, 6:6, but the waw-prefixed spelling is 1 book-wide (sweep --skel וכען: oshb:Ezra.5.17 alone). The 6 belongs to the bare skeleton (sweep --skel כען: oshb:Ezra.4.13, oshb:Ezra.4.14, oshb:Ezra.4.21, oshb:Ezra.5.16, oshb:Ezra.5.17, oshb:Ezra.6.6), and two members of that set are not requests or directives in the row's sense: oshb:Ezra.5.16 has «וּמִן אֱדַ֧יִן וְעַד כְּעַ֛ן», temporal 'and from then until now' inside the reported reply, and oshb:Ezra.6.6 opens with «כְּעַ֡ן», waw-less and introducing a royal order rather than a request.
challenges.suggested_action: Attach the count to the string actually swept (skeleton כען, 6 book-wide), drop 5:16 from the request/directive class, and note that the spelling this row quotes is unique to 5:17 — which sharpens rather than weakens the register-shift reading of the back edge.

challenges.claim: 'One speaker' is not what the text shows, and a stronger rival than the one named is available. The 1cp changes referent inside the letter: at oshb:Ezra.5.9 and oshb:Ezra.5.10 «שְׁאֵ֨לְנָא֙» / «שְׁאֵ֥לְנָא» is the inspecting party (web:Ezra.5.9 “Then we asked those elders”), whereas oshb:Ezra.5.11 introduces the answer with a speech frame, «וּכְנֵ֥מָא פִתְגָמָ֖א הֲתִיב֣וּנָא לְמֵמַ֑ר», after which «אֲנַ֣חְנָא הִמּ֡וֹ עַבְדוֹהִי֩» is the builders' own 1cp (web:Ezra.5.11 “We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth”). That inset carries an introduction formula and a resumption after it at oshb:Ezra.5.17 — the double frame the strategy's inset rule names as the split test — and its terminus is genuinely contestable, since nothing in the pointed text closes the quotation (WEB's punctuation, a translator's choice and not evidence, keeps it open to the end of 5:17). The rejected alternative instead names the 5:8/5:17 rhetorical pivot, which no frame formula marks.
challenges.suggested_action: Defend the whole-letter reading against the framed inset at 5:11-5:16 rather than against an unframed rhetorical pivot, and replace the 'single speaker' premise with the accurate one: a single sender and a single addressee hosting a quoted reply.

challenges.claim: The '3 times book-wide' figure is idiom-scoped but is attached in the prose to the jussive form. The jussive alone stands in 6 verses (sweep --skel להוא: oshb:Ezra.4.12, oshb:Ezra.4.13, oshb:Ezra.5.8, oshb:Ezra.6.9, oshb:Ezra.7.23, oshb:Ezra.7.26); only the two-word disclosure idiom is 3 (sweep --skel ידיע להוא: oshb:Ezra.4.12, oshb:Ezra.4.13, oshb:Ezra.5.8). One of the four remaining sits inside this cluster at oshb:Ezra.6.9, «לֶהֱוֵ֨א מִתְיְהֵ֥ב», where the same jussive carries a standing supply order and discloses nothing.
challenges.suggested_action: Name the swept string (skeleton ידיע להוא, 3 book-wide) so the figure is not read as a count of the jussive.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both edges are tier-1 and clean: 5:6's copy-formula matches the strategy's own byte-verified specimen for this device exactly, and 5:17's closing petition hands off cleanly to 6:1's בֵּאדַ֛יִן. The rejected alternative -- splitting at the 5:8|5:17 report/petition seam -- is fairly stated as a genuine rhetorical distinction that nonetheless shares one speaker and one addressee with no re-opening incipit; the interior marks in 5:7-5:15 are all weak samekh (undisclosed, but none strong enough to complicate that call). The two quantitative claims in this row both check out against an independent sweep.

The repair's decisive warrant is a new absence claim carried twice with no sweep and no defined marker class: the rationale ends the inset argument with "no textual marker closes this quoted reply before Ezra.5.17's own petition resumes", and the rejected-alternative defeats the strongest rival with the same words. Nothing in the row says what would count as a closing marker, and the same letter supplies a counterexample two verses earlier: oshb:Ezra.5.9 introduces a quoted question with כְּנֵ֖מָא אֲמַ֣רְנָא לְּהֹ֑ם and oshb:Ezra.5.10 simply resumes Tattenai's 1cp report, וְאַ֧ף שְׁמָהָתְהֹ֛ם שְׁאֵ֥לְנָא לְּהֹ֖ם (web:Ezra.5.10 "We asked them their names also"), with no closing marker whatever. Absence of a closing marker therefore does not separate an inset that has ended from one still running. The same sentence also concedes that 5:17's petition "resumes" - which is the second prong (introduction formula AND a resumption after) of the strategy-draft inset test the row expressly invokes, so the rival is dismissed on a prong the row's own clause grants. (+1 further finding(s); see challenges)

challenges.claim: The repaired sweep gloss under-corrects by one. v0 said the particle "recurs 6 times book-wide framing requests or directives"; v1 keeps the six-verse sweep (independently confirmed: bare-form skeleton sweep returns exactly Ezra.4.13, 4.14, 4.21, 5.16, 5.17, 6.6) and subtracts only 5:16 as temporal, concluding "leaving 5 of the 6 actually framing requests or directives". Ezra.4.14 frames neither: its particle heads a causal ground clause whose main verbs are perfects reporting the senders' own completed action, עַ֨ל דְּנָ֔ה שְׁלַ֖חְנָא וְהוֹדַ֥עְנָא לְמַלְכָּֽא (web:Ezra.4.14 "therefore we have sent and informed the king,"). On the row's own criterion the figure is 4 of 6 - 4:13 jussive disclosure, 4:21 imperative, 5:17 petition, 6:6 directive - so the repair fixes one miscounted member of the class and leaves another of the same kind standing.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate as 4 of the 6, or widen the criterion to something 4:14 satisfies (e.g. "opens the letter's operative move") and say which. The 5:17 register-shift point survives either way, and the waw-prefixed uniqueness claim needs no change - confirmed at 1 book-wide occurrence, Ezra.5.17.

primary_reviews.rationale: I reproduced the opener sweep independently: the skeleton (sweep --skel באדין) stands in 3 verses, oshb:Ezra.4.24, oshb:Ezra.5.2 and oshb:Ezra.6.1, so the count carried at oshb:Ezra.6.1 is exact. The quotation-introducing formula is in fact better evidence than the row claims. At oshb:Ezra.5.7 «וְכִדְנָה֙ כְּתִ֣יב בְּגַוֵּ֔הּ» has a 3ms suffix agreeing with the masculine «פִּתְגָמָ֖א», while at oshb:Ezra.6.2 «וְכֵן כְּתִ֥יב בְּגַוַּ֖הּ דִּכְרוֹנָֽה» has a 3fs suffix agreeing with the feminine «מְגִלָּ֣ה חֲדָ֑ה» that was found in the archive: one formula inflecting to its own antecedent, which is a stronger identification of a shared device than the bare word-match asserted. The interior era-formula at oshb:Ezra.6.3 is the obvious place to hunt for an unargued tier-1 seam, and the row disposes of it correctly by treating 6:3-6:5 as content quoted under the colon-formula of oshb:Ezra.6.2; that disposal is independently confirmed at oshb:Ezra.5.13, where «בִּשְׁנַ֣ת חֲדָ֔ה לְכ֥וֹרֶשׁ מַלְכָּ֖א» followed by «כּ֤וֹרֶשׁ מַלְכָּא֙ שָׂ֣ם טְעֵ֔ם» reproduces nearly the whole formula mid-letter and opens nothing. The back edge is the clean kind — oshb:Ezra.6.6 changes speaker, addressee and person together. I record the whole mark picture for the span as weak corroboration that drives nothing: pmarks_Ezra.json (single-witness, WLC) has SAMEKH after Ezra.5.17 at the front edge, PE after Ezra.6.2 inside the span, and SAMEKH after Ezra.6.5 at the back edge. Each quoted form in the row collated at byte tier.

The core call is sound: the 3-instance book-wide count for בֵּאדַ֛יִן is independently reproduced, and the 6:2 / 5:7 כְּתִ֣יב בְּגַוֵּ֔הּ parallel is a real and useful cross-reference rather than an assumed one. The Cyrus record's third-person voicing, correctly contrasted against Darius's 1cs at 6:12 in the sibling row, is accurate on inspection -- there is no 1cs self-naming anywhere in 6:3-5. But this row sits exactly on the kind of inset attach/detach call the brief flags for scrutiny (archive memo + embedded decree copy), and it omits an available tier-3 signal bearing directly on the internal seam it argues against.

primary_reviews.rationale: Two of the three load-bearing claims check out. The closing self-identification at oshb:Ezra.6.12, «אֲנָ֤ה דָרְיָ֨וֶשׁ֙ שָׂ֣מֶת טְעֵ֔ם», is a 1cs perfect with the king's name in apposition, and no 1cs form occurs anywhere in oshb:Ezra.6.3-oshb:Ezra.6.5, so 'no counterpart in the quoted Cyrus record' is true as scoped. The funding clause at oshb:Ezra.6.8 is also read correctly as directive: the prefix form there is 3fs, agreeing with the feminine noun for the outlay, and it pairs with a passive participle, which is the ordinary way of ordering a disbursement in this block. What fails is the discriminator used to open the unit. The front edge survives that failure, since oshb:Ezra.6.6 supplies named addressees and a second-person imperative absent from the archived memo.

challenges.claim: The stated discriminator is false to the text: the quoted memo is itself in command register. The row opens the unit on 'a direct command register wholly absent from the third-person quoted memo of 6:3-6:5', but that memo is a decree — «שָׂ֣ם טְעֵם֒» at oshb:Ezra.6.3 — whose content is carried by prefix-conjugation directives from end to end: «בַּיְתָ֣א יִתְבְּנֵ֔א» there, «וְנִ֨פְקְתָ֔א מִן בֵּ֥ית מַלְכָּ֖א תִּתְיְהִֽב» at oshb:Ezra.6.4, and «יַהֲתִיב֗וּן וִ֠יהָךְ» closing with «וְתַחֵ֖ת» at oshb:Ezra.6.5, a t-prefix form (2ms, or 3fs) that this cluster's own row M8-Ezra-027 cites from web:Ezra.6.5 as “You shall put them in God's house.” What actually changes at oshb:Ezra.6.6 is person and addressee: «רַחִיקִ֥ין הֲו֖וֹ» is a 2mp imperative of the verb 'to be' with a predicate participle, aimed at officials named in the vocative.
challenges.suggested_action: Recast the opening argument as a person-and-addressee shift — unaddressed third-person directives in the archived memo versus a 2mp imperative with named addressees — instead of presence versus absence of a command register; the 6:5|6:6 boundary is unaffected by the correction.

primary_reviews.rationale: Every element checks out against source: the 6:8 funding jussive, the impalement curse at 6:11, and the 1cs self-naming closing formula at 6:12 are all present exactly as quoted. The claim that no 1cs self-naming appears anywhere in the quoted Cyrus record (6:3-5) is correct on inspection, not asserted on faith, and it is the row's real warrant rather than decoration. Both edges -- 6:6's addressee shift out of the third-person memo, and 6:12's self-naming answered by 6:13's confirmed scene-onset particle -- are independently argued rather than borrowed wholesale from the neighboring rows.

The replacement warrant is contradicted by the evidence quoted in the same sentence. v1 concludes "unaddressed 3rd-person directives in the archived memo give way to a 2mp imperative naming living officials", but the 6:5 clause it has just quoted ends וְתַחֵ֖ת בְּבֵ֥ית אֱלָהָֽא, which the row itself glosses "you shall put" and which web:Ezra.6.5 renders "You shall put them in God's house." That is a second-person addressed directive inside the memo, so the memo is neither uniformly third-person nor unaddressed, and person does not cleanly change at 6:6 either (2ms in 6:5 to 2mp in 6:6). The single ellipsized gloss "let them be restored...you shall put" spans three clauses of differing person, which blurs exactly the distribution the new argument turns on. challenges.claim: The 6:12|6:13 seam is now held to two different evidentiary standards by the two rows that share it. Row 029's repair supplies the function-separated count for the אֱ֠דַיִן family (8 tokens across 7 non-בֵּאדַ֛יִן-type verses) and argues 6:13's local discourse role, which is what the strategy draft's Aramaic-zone discipline requires of anyone citing either form at a seam. Row 028's rejected-alternative still decides its own rear seam on "oshb:Ezra.6.13's confirmed scene-onset" with no count, no local-role argument, and an unexplained "confirmed" - the lexeme alone, the one thing that section forbids.
challenges.suggested_action: Bring 028's rear-seam sentence into line with 029: cite the function-separated count once, state 6:13's local role (compliance narration at host-account level, outside any quoted document), and drop "confirmed".

primary_reviews.rationale: The ketiv/qere disclosure is accurate: OSHB carries the pair adjacent at oshb:Ezra.6.14, «נביאה נְבִיָּ֔א», replicating one of the two pairs carried at oshb:Ezra.5.1; the row discloses that pair where its quotation crosses it, as strategy §4 requires. The date colophon at oshb:Ezra.6.15 is byte-exact and its closing function is not in question. Two supporting claims fail on inspection and are challenged below; one device label is also loose — the prophet-echo between 5:1 and 6:14 brackets the building account down to the completion notice, not 'this part', which runs on to oshb:Ezra.6.22, and 6:14 sits mid-span here, so it cannot frame this row either. On calibration I record, without treating it as a driver, that the witness signal near the downgraded back edge falls exactly on it: pmarks_Ezra.json (single-witness, WLC) has PE after Ezra.6.12 at the front edge and PE after Ezra.6.15 at the back edge, with no mark inside the span. Tier-3 cannot lift that edge, but the row grades it down without recording what does sit there.

challenges.claim: The particle sweep does not match its own enumeration, and it drops the token this campaign has already corrected once. The row states '7 book-wide' and then lists six verses (4:9, 4:23, 5:4, 5:9, 5:16, 6:13), omitting oshb:Ezra.5.5 — «וֶאֱדַ֛יִן» — which decision M8-Ezra-025 quotes in this same cluster. Swept independently, the skeleton (sweep --skel אדין) stands in 10 verses, three of them the compound set (sweep --skel באדין: oshb:Ezra.4.24, oshb:Ezra.5.2, oshb:Ezra.6.1), leaving seven — oshb:Ezra.4.9, oshb:Ezra.4.23, oshb:Ezra.5.4, oshb:Ezra.5.5, oshb:Ezra.5.9, oshb:Ezra.5.16, oshb:Ezra.6.13 — and oshb:Ezra.5.16 carries two tokens, «אֱדַ֨יִן֙» and «וּמִן אֱדַ֧יִן», so the total is 8 tokens in 7 verses.
challenges.suggested_action: Restore 5:5 to the enumeration and state whether the figure counts verses (7) or tokens (8), disclosing 5:16's double the way multi-mark verses are disclosed elsewhere.

challenges.claim: The contrast that grades 6:13's particle above its rivals is not true of the text. The row argues that 'unlike 5:9 and 5:16's mid-letter narration uses, 6:13's stands verse-initial', yet both comparanda are themselves verse-initial: oshb:Ezra.5.9 begins «אֱדַ֗יִן שְׁאֵ֨לְנָא֙» and oshb:Ezra.5.16 begins «אֱדַ֨יִן֙ שֵׁשְׁבַּצַּ֣ר», each opening its own verse. The difference is level, not position — 5:9 and 5:16 narrate inside the quoted letter while 6:13 narrates in the host account — and the row's own phrase 'mid-letter narration' already carries that.
challenges.suggested_action: Delete the verse-initial contrast and let the host-level versus letter-internal distinction do the work; the front edge does not need the false half of the argument.

primary_reviews.rationale: The compliance-onset argument at 6:13 is sound on its own terms: the bare אֱ֠דַיִן stands verse-initial here, unlike its mid-letter appearances at 5:9 and 5:16, and the row argues that functional contrast rather than the lexeme alone -- exactly the discipline strategy section 4 requires. The 6:14 ketiv/qere and the 5:1 prophetic inclusio are both accurate on inspection. The row is also commendably honest about its own weak back edge (6:15|6:16), correctly matching strategy section 7's designation of that seam as low-confidence, and medium_low is the right call for that reason alone. The problem is narrower: the sweep citation backing the '7 book-wide' claim is short one member.

challenges.claim: The row states the bare אֱ֠דַיִן-type particle is found '7 book-wide' but its parenthetical sweep citation lists only 6 refs (4.9, 4.23, 5.4, 5.9, 5.16, 6.13), omitting Ezra.5.5's וֶאֱדַ֛יִן -- the token strategy section 4 explicitly flags as previously missed and re-verified. challenges.suggested_action: Add oshb:Ezra.5.5 to both the parenthetical sweep citation and boundary_evidence_refs so the disclosed list matches the asserted count of 7.

primary_reviews.rationale: Nothing in oshb:Ezra.6.16 is labelled with grammar foreign to it, which is what has to be checked on a row sitting at the end of the block: the determined plurals «כָּהֲנַיָּ֨א וְלֵוָיֵ֜א» and the determined «גָלוּתָ֗א» are what a communal subject looks like here. The row's back edge is the strongest seam in this cluster and it is stated modestly: the scriptural-citation formula closes oshb:Ezra.6.18, which is also where the block's language terminates, and the next verse restarts narration with a newly named festival and a fresh calendar date. The front edge is the weak one, as the row concedes; my objection is that the contrast propping it misreports the two verses before it.

challenges.claim: The subject contrast overstates what 6:13-6:15 contains. The row — and the mirrored sentence in M8-Ezra-029's rejected alternative — says the preceding unit 'names officials alone', but oshb:Ezra.6.14 makes the Judean elders its subject, «וְשָׂבֵ֤י יְהוּדָיֵא֙ בָּנַ֣יִן וּמַצְלְחִ֔ין» (web:Ezra.6.14 “The elders of the Jews built and prospered”), and oshb:Ezra.6.15 makes the building itself the subject, «וְשֵׁיצִיא֙ בַּיְתָ֣ה דְנָ֔ה» (web:Ezra.6.15 “This house was finished”). What oshb:Ezra.6.16 does is broaden an already-Judean subject to the assembled community; it does not replace Persian officials with Israelites, so the sharpest form of the contrast is unavailable and this weak edge is left resting on the change of topic to «חֲנֻכַּ֛ת» alone.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate the edge as a broadening of subject plus a change of topic, and drop 'names officials alone'; if the topic change is all that remains, the medium confidence deserves re-examination against the 029 row that shares this seam.

primary_reviews.rationale: The subject/topic-shift argument (whole community plus חֲנֻכַּ֛ת against 6:13-15's officials-only completion notice) is the right kind of tier-1 signal even without a strong discourse particle, and the row is transparent that this is the weaker of its two edges -- consistent with its sibling row's identical honesty about the same seam from the other side. The Aramaic-zone close at 6:18, immediately preceding 6:19's language switch, is correctly identified as the terminus of the whole 4:8-6:18 zone.

The repair corrects a real v0 error but leaves the front seam weaker than the row admits. v0 contrasted "the whole community, not the officials of 6:13-6.15"; v1 concedes that 6:14's subject is already a Judean corporate body, וְשָׂבֵ֤י יְהוּדָיֵא֙ בָּנַ֣יִן וּמַצְלְחִ֔ין (web:Ezra.6.14 "The elders of the Jews built and prospered"), and that 6:15's subject is the building. The preceding row therefore contains two subject changes of its own (officials, elders, building), so subject change cannot be the seam criterion in this stretch and "broadening" is reduced to a difference of degree - at an edge the row itself calls the weaker of the unit's two, with confidence frozen at medium. The one categorical discriminator left, the new topic חֲנֻכַּ֛ת (dedication), is stated but no longer carries the sentence.

The preceding row therefore contains two subject changes of its own (officials, elders, building), so subject change cannot be the seam criterion in this stretch and "broadening" is reduced to a difference of degree - at an edge the row itself calls the weaker of the unit's two, with confidence frozen at medium. Row 029's rejected-alternative carries the same reasoning and should move with it.

boss_ruling.reasoning: The subject inventory of 6:13-15 (elders build and complete; the house stands finished) replaces the officials-only description on both this row and 029's mirrored sentence.

primary_reviews.rationale: The verb-form label is right here and would have been a defect three verses earlier, since the block's language terminates with 6:18 and oshb:Ezra.6.19 is Hebrew: «וַיַּעֲשׂ֥וּ» is a wayyiqtol. I traced the chain the row claims and it is there — «וַיַּעֲשׂ֥וּ» (6:19), «וַיִּשְׁחֲט֤וּ» (6:20), «וַיֹּאכְל֣וּ» (6:21), «וַיַּֽעֲשׂ֧וּ» (6:22) — with one nuance worth recording rather than challenging: the purification itself is carried by a subordinate causal clause, «כִּ֣י הִֽטַּהֲר֞וּ», not by the chain, which resumes inside the same verse. The switch is argued as a bundle (fresh verb chain, newly named festival, new calendar date) rather than as a bare change of language, which is what the tier-1 rule demands. On rival quality I probed the obvious interior split between the Passover of 6:19-6:21 and the seven-day feast of «וַיַּֽעֲשׂ֧וּ חַג מַצּ֛וֹת שִׁבְעַ֥ת יָמִ֖ים», the larger-unit test the strategy names: the body does engage it, arguing that the closing theological clause seals one notice rather than two, even though the rejected-alternative slot spends itself on backward attachment. Every form sliced for this row matched the source bytes exactly.

This is the cleanest row in the cluster: the language-switch-as-bundle argument (wayyiqtol chain plus new festival plus new calendar date, not the language switch alone) is exactly the discipline strategy section 1 requires for language-switch seams, and it is argued rather than merely asserted. The 6:22 theological summary clause is a legitimate closural device, and the rejected alternative -- treating 6:19 as a continuation of the dedication festivities -- is fairly stated and correctly defeated by the same co-occurring signal bundle rather than by the language switch in isolation.

primary_reviews.rationale: The syntactic analysis is the strongest part of this row and it is correct: oshb:Ezra.7.1-oshb:Ezra.7.5 carries no finite predicate for Ezra at all — the era phrase is followed by a name and an unbroken chain of «בֶּן» — and oshb:Ezra.7.6 resumes the suspended clause with «ה֤וּא עֶזְרָא֙ עָלָ֣ה מִבָּבֶ֔ל», so the genealogy is a dependent extraposition rather than a register with its own incipit, and the rejected alternative disposes of the 7:1-5 rival on the right grounds. Mark handling is accurate and symmetric: pmarks_Ezra.json (single-witness, WLC) has PE after Ezra.6.22 and PE after Ezra.7.6, both disclosed, and no mark falls inside Ezra.7.1-Ezra.7.5, so nothing is withheld. My objection is confined to the close, where the row itself defers the driver to the following row.

challenges.claim: The close is argued from a broadening that the next two verses withdraw. «וַיַּֽעֲל֣וּ» at oshb:Ezra.7.7 does widen the subject for one verse, but oshb:Ezra.7.8 returns to the singular, «וַיָּבֹ֥א יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם» (web:Ezra.7.8 “He came to Jerusalem in the fifth month”), and oshb:Ezra.7.9 keeps Ezra singular while repeating this row's own closing lexeme: «עָלָ֣ה מִבָּבֶ֔ל» at 7:6 answers to «ה֣וּא יְסֻ֔ד הַֽמַּעֲלָ֖ה מִבָּבֶ֑ל» at 7:9 (web:Ezra.7.9 “he began to go up from Babylon”). Verses 7:6-7:9 therefore read as one dated ascent report whose participants oscillate, so a participant shift at 7:7 is not durable enough to close a unit, and what is left holding this edge is a tier-3 mark (PE after Ezra.7.6, pmarks_Ezra.json, single-witness) that by rule cannot drive it.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue the 7:6|7:7 seam from something internal to it — the completion of the extraposition-and-resumption sentence at 7:6 is the natural candidate — or reopen the 7:1-7:10 unit test, since the broadening at 7:7 does not survive into 7:8.

primary_reviews.rationale: The extraposition-and-resumption syntax argument is the strongest single piece of grammar in this cluster: the unbroken 'ben X' genealogical chain from 7:1 through 7:5 to Aaron, resumed by the independent pronoun and repeated name ה֤וּא עֶזְרָא֙ at 7:6, is confirmed against source and correctly identifies the genealogy as syntactically bound rather than a free-standing list -- exactly the right basis for keeping it out of the strategy's list-inset category. The row's pmark discipline is also the cluster's best: both the 6:22 and 7:6 PE marks are disclosed, correctly labeled single-witness, and correctly subordinated to the era formula as the actual driver rather than cited as if they carried weight. My objection is at the back edge, which the row explicitly declines to argue on its own terms.

challenges.claim: The row's own back-edge warrant for stopping at 7:6 is not argued within this row: the rationale states 'the driving signal is that 7:7 broadens the acting subject from Ezra alone to the wider company (argued in the next row)', deferring the entire close-edge test to a decision outside this dossier. Strategy section 6 itself describes 7:1-10 as one descriptive span ('Ezra genealogy+arrival 7:1-10') without naming an internal sub-seam the way it does for every other block in the same section, which is at minimum ambiguous about whether 7:6|7:7 was meant to be a decision boundary at all.
challenges.suggested_action: Supply this row's own independent warrant for the 7:6|7:7 boundary -- for instance 7:6's closing notice that 'the king granted him all his request' as a summarizing cadence in its own right -- rather than relying entirely on the sibling row's evidence; or, if the warrant genuinely lives only at 7:7, reconsider whether 7:1-6 is separable from 7:7-10 at all.

primary_reviews.rationale: All three Hebrew citations here return byte tier and the semantic reading of the two subordinating clauses is right: 7:9 and 7:10 are both explanatory, and the turn at 7:10 from itinerary to Ezra's own resolve is a fair place to stop. What does not survive inspection is the verb-form warrant offered at the front edge. The chapter's wayyiqtol sequence has already begun one verse earlier and it does not break where the row implies. Participant-widening, which the row also names, is a legitimate tier-1 scene-and-participant signal and can carry the seam by itself, but as the rationale is written the leading grammatical argument points the other way. The rejected alternative is also under-powered: the rival it names has a lexical argument available to it that the row leaves unanswered. Marks are typed correctly, keyed to the right verses, and labelled single-witness, and the PE at 7:6 is properly held back from driving anything. Medium confidence sits about right, perhaps a shade generous once the verb argument is withdrawn.

challenges.claim: The opening warrant, that 7:7 reopens the wayyiqtol chain, is contradicted by the verse immediately before the claimed seam. oshb:Ezra.7.6 already ends its sentence with a wayyiqtol, וַיִּתֶּן, rendered “and the king granted him” (web:Ezra.7.6), and the sequence carries on past 7:7 into oshb:Ezra.7.8 וַיָּבֹ֥א. So the chain runs from 7:6b through 7:8 and it gives way at 7:9 to a subordinating כִּ֗י, well inside this row. 7:7's וַיַּֽעֲל֣וּ is continuative across the front seam rather than resumptive at it, which means the verbal syntax argues for continuity at exactly the join the row is trying to open. Tier-1 participant change (Israel, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants replacing Ezra alone as subject) does hold the seam, but no other signal now supports it.
challenges.suggested_action: Withdraw or restate the “reopens the wayyiqtol chain” clause and rest the front edge on the participant-widening alone; if the verbal chain is discussed at all, add oshb:Ezra.7.8 to the evidence refs so the sequence can be seen to end inside the row.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative does not meet the rival's best evidence. The hand-of-God formula stands at the very end of oshb:Ezra.7.6, כְּיַד יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהָיו֙ עָלָ֔יו, and again at the very end of oshb:Ezra.7.9, כְּיַד אֱלֹהָ֖יו הַטּוֹבָ֥ה עָלָֽיו; sweep.py --skel כיד returns 4 occurrences book-wide (7:6, 7:9, 7:28, 8:18). A reader arguing that 7:7-10 belongs with the introduction can therefore point to a repeated clause-final formula that straddles the 7:6|7:7 join, and the row's reply — that 7:7-10 is a self-contained chronological-and-motivational unit — does not touch it.
challenges.suggested_action: Answer the bracket on the record, for instance by showing that the formula is a motif the memoir carries forward to 7:28 rather than a unit-closing device, and mirror oshb:Ezra.7.9's instance against the 7:6 instance in the argument.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both edges hold. The front seam is a genuine participant/scene broadening: 7:6 is a disjunctive qatal clause naming Ezra alone (הוא עזרא עלה), while 7:7's ויצזעלו is the chapter's first true wayyiqtol, resuming the narrative chain (dormant since 6:22) with priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants added to the traveling party. The back seam at 7:11 is a strong, matrix-attested document-copy incipit. The two כי clauses in 7:9-10 read as one chronological-then-motivational unit, and the rejected alternative (folding into a ten-verse intro) is the real rival here, correctly declined.

The other side of the same contradiction, actionable in this row's own terms. The repair reduces the front seam to one signal - "the front seam rests on this participant-widening, not on the wayyiqtol chain" - after conceding that the chain runs unbroken across that very seam (verified: וַיִּתֶּן 7:6, וַיַּֽעֲל֣וּ 7:7, וַיָּבֹ֥א 7:8, break only at 7:9). The neighbouring row 032, whose rear seam is this same edge, states in its repaired rationale that this participant-widening "does not durably distinguish 7:6 from what follows". This row's sole surviving warrant is thus the one its neighbour rejects, while the concession it adds is the one its neighbour's cadence claim denies; confidence here is frozen at medium.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both citations collate at byte tier, and each is labelled with the language proper to its side of the switch: 7:11 is the Hebrew narrator's copy formula, 7:12 the Aramaic salutation, and the determined-state reading of מַלְכַיָּ֑א is exactly right. The close is in fact better founded than the row troubles to argue. וּכְעֶֽנֶת stands as the final word of its verse at every occurrence in the book (sweep.py --skel כענת: 3 occurrences book-wide, at 4:10, 4:11 and 7:12), and the shorter variant at oshb:Ezra.4.17, וּכְעֶֽת, is likewise verse-final; Ezra's own epistolary usage thus puts the praescriptio hinge at the end of the address section and the body in the following verse, which is precisely where this row cuts. My reservation is at the other end. The 7:11|7:12 junction is the one place in this cluster where two strategy provisions pull against each other, and the row settles it by citing just the one that favours its own span. The single witness's paragraphing also happens to fall there, and goes unmentioned.

challenges.claim: The row resolves the Hebrew-to-Aramaic junction inside its own span by the inset rule alone, without acknowledging that the device matrix independently lists 7:12 as one of the book's four tier-1 language-switch seams (switch plus rescript frame). The same junction is therefore named boundary-driving by one provision and non-boundary by another, and the row engages neither the conflict nor the rival that follows from it — 7:11 standing alone as the Hebrew narrator's notice with the letter beginning at 7:12. The rival actually named runs the opposite way, toward merging the whole rescript. Corroborating this at tier 3 and no higher: pmarks_Ezra.json (single-witness) places a PE after Ezra.7.11, which makes it 1 of 2 marks interior to a row across this cluster's 8 spans — the other, after Ezra.8.1, is disclosed by the row containing it, whereas this one is passed over in silence while 4 of the 8 rows disclose their edge marks freely. A Writings mark can neither move this seam nor count against it by absence, so this is a disclosure and argument-completeness point; but with the strongest rival unnamed, “high” confidence is hard to sustain.
challenges.suggested_action: Disclose the interior PE at Ezra.7.11 as tier-3 single-witness weak corroboration for the rival, argue the switch-seam provision explicitly against the inset rule instead of citing just the latter, and either name 7:11-alone as the strongest rejected alternative or drop the confidence to medium.

primary_reviews.rationale: The Aramaic behaves as described. מִנִּי֮ שִׂ֣ים טְעֵם֒ is the standing decree formula of this book's rescripts — sweep.py --skel שים טעם: 6 occurrences book-wide (4:19, 5:17, 6:8, 6:11, 7:13, 7:21) — the כָּל קֳבֵ֗ל דִּי֩ of 7:14 is genuinely causal, and the claim that 7:15 extends the same purpose construction is exact: וּלְהֵיבָלָ֖ה coordinates with 7:14's לְבַקָּרָ֥א under one and the same passive participle שְׁלִ֔יחַ. 7:16's וְכֹל֙ כְּסַ֣ף וּדְהַ֔ב continues that infinitive's object chain, which is good reason to keep 15 and 16 in one row. I pressed the front-to-back cohesion question too: 7:17's בְּכַסְפָּ֣א דְנָ֗ה is anaphoric to what 7:15-16 has just named, so there is real linkage over the closing seam — but anaphora is exactly what a source-to-use pivot predicts, and it does not argue for continuity. What is defective is confined to the one-sentence rival, which names a span its cited source does not contain and rebuts a signal that is not there.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative misattributes its own rival and then rebuts a phantom. The strategy's block map gives 7:11-26 as the coarse rescript span and contains no 7:13-20 decree-body span, so there is no “block map's one undifferentiated decree-body span” of that shape to reject. The contrast then drawn with “a modern translator's paragraph break” has no referent either: WEB runs 7:13-20 unbroken and its paragraph breaks in this chapter fall at 7:21, 7:24 and 7:25, not at 7:17 (offered here as tier-4 metadata, to show that the row's own tier-4 contrast is empty and not as boundary evidence in either direction). The substantive ground, the shift within the kol-qevel idiom, is sound and stands without either prop.

Nothing in the warrant-touching edits here trips any checklist class.

primary_reviews.rationale: The pivot this row identifies is real, and a book-wide count can be put behind it: sweep.py --skel כל קבל: 3 occurrences book-wide (4:14, 7:14, 7:17); at oshb:Ezra.4.14 and oshb:Ezra.7.14 the idiom takes the relativizer and heads a causal clause, while 7:17 alone takes the demonstrative and heads an inferential directive. So the function of the idiom does change exactly where the front seam is placed, and the row's description of that change is accurate Aramaic. The interior holds together as a disbursement sequence, and 7:20's closing draw on the treasury is quoted correctly. The rejected alternative, however, misstates the grammar of the very verse it uses to justify the close — and the correction runs in the row's favour, which is why medium_low now looks too low.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative says 7:21 “addresses a distinct, named class of officials in the third person”. It does not. The treasurers are named in a prepositional phrase, oshb:Ezra.7.21 לְכֹל֙ גִּזַּֽבְרַיָּ֔א, and the same verse then speaks to them directly with a second-plural object suffix, oshb:Ezra.7.21 יִ֠שְׁאֲלֶנְכוֹן, “requires of you” (web:Ezra.7.21); the plural address continues at oshb:Ezra.7.24 וּלְכֹ֣ם, “Also we inform you” (web:Ezra.7.24). Nor is the contrast a simple singular-to-plural one, because plural address is already present inside this row at oshb:Ezra.7.18, אֱלָהֲכֹ֖ם with תַּעַבְדֽוּן, alongside singular reference to Ezra (the singular forms there stand as ketiv/qere pairs and are disclosed, not quoted); 7:19-20 then return to the singular, oshb:Ezra.7.19 לָ֔ךְ and אֱלָהָ֑ךְ. What changes at 7:20|7:21 is the referent of the address — from Ezra's party to a freshly named class of officials — not the grammatical person.
challenges.suggested_action: Replace “in the third person” with the referent-shift description, demonstrated from the second-plural suffixes of 7:21 and 7:24; because that reading makes the close firmer than the row currently claims, reconsider the confidence upward from medium_low.

primary_reviews.rationale: The internal grammar is precisely observed — DI versus DENAH correctly distinguished and tied to a causal-to-inferential shift — and the row's own medium_low label already signals appropriate caution; it is the one row in the cluster that grades its own weakest link honestly. But the device doing the boundary work here doesn't land in any tier-1 category the brief enumerates: no addressee change (Ezra remains 'you' throughout 7:13-20), no scene/participant/location change, no frame formula, no language switch. What's argued is a within-decree topic pivot inferred from a single particle contrast — a real literary observation, but not self-evidently tier-1, unlike the treasurer-address shift two rows later (037) or the Ezra-vocative two rows after that (038), both squarely participant-shift seams in the same decree.

primary_reviews.rationale: Front edge: unobjectionable. The three Aramaic citations collate byte-exact, the emphatic independent pronoun is correctly identified, and the readdressing of the decree to the treasurers beyond the River is a genuine tier-1 participant change rather than a topical one. The interior is described accurately, including the exemption vocabulary of 7:24. Two things weaken the packet without touching the span. The one-sentence rival is dismissed on a premise the Aramaic contradicts, since 7:24 does open with an attested announcement formula; and the row reaches past the nearer, closer comparandum for its resumption device to a verse whose titulature is not in fact repeated. Neither defect threatens the boundaries, so high confidence still seems to me defensible.

challenges.claim: The rival split at 7:23|7:24 is rejected on the stated ground that no intervening frame device separates the two blocks, but 7:24 opens with the book's own letter-internal announcement formula: oshb:Ezra.7.24 וּלְכֹ֣ם מְהוֹדְעִ֗ין, which the row itself renders “Also we inform you” (web:Ezra.7.24). sweep.py --skel מהודע: 2 occurrences book-wide, at 4:16 and 7:24, and at oshb:Ezra.4.16 the same participle carries an explicit 1cp pronoun, מְהוֹדְעִ֤ין אֲנַ֨חְנָה֙, where it opens that letter's decisive announcement. The formula also moves the speaker off the singular royal self-reference of oshb:Ezra.7.21 אֲנָ֞ה. A twice-attested announcement formula is at minimum a candidate frame device, so the rival is dismissed on a factual premise the text does not support.
challenges.suggested_action: Reject the 7:24 split on the ground that is actually available — that the formula introduces a further provision to the same named addressee rather than a new addressee or a new genre — and cite oshb:Ezra.4.16 as the controlling in-book parallel.

primary_reviews.rationale: I probed both edges and both held. At the opening the signal is the cleanest in the whole rescript: oshb:Ezra.7.25 fronts an independent second-person pronoun with a vocative name, וְאַ֣נְתְּ עֶזְרָ֗א, and the suffixes immediately revert to the singular, אֱלָהָ֤ךְ and בִידָךְ֙, after the plural-addressed treasurer material. The strongest counter-pressure I could find is lexical: 7:24's announcement participle and 7:25's closing תְּהוֹדְעֽוּן share a root and the closing form is itself plural. That does not rescue a merger, because a shared root across a join is not a unit signal when an explicit vocative stands at the join, and the plural at the end of 7:25 attaches to the magistrates who are to be taught, not to the treasurers. The close is equally well handled. Identifying לֶהֱוֵ֥א מִתְעֲבֵ֖ד as jussive in force is correct, and the row selected the right one of the verse's two such forms — the earlier לֶהֱוֵ֨א עָבֵ֜ד in the protasis is periphrastic, and quoting that one would have been the error. The PE at 7:26 is correctly typed, flagged single-witness, and used strictly as weak corroboration, which is the right treatment for Writings. Two ketiv/qere pairs sit inside this span, at 7:25 and 7:26, but neither Aramaic citation spans one, so the strategy's disclosure trigger is not tripped. If anything medium understates how firm this row is.

The vocative reopening ('ואנת עזרא', 'You, Ezra') is a real, clean tier-1 addressee return and is well argued. But the row folds two distinguishable speech-acts into one span without testing the finer split: 7:25 is Ezra's own commissioning charge, while 7:26 is a self-contained casuistic enactment with its own protasis-apodosis shape ('whoever will not do... let it be done to him') — and protasis-apodosis is itself a tier-1 category the brief names outright. The row's rejected alternative only tests backward attachment to 7:21-24, never this interior 7:25/7:26 split.

challenges.claim: 7:26 opens its own protasis-apodosis clause (כל די לא להוא עבד...להוא מתעבד מנה with its own penalty triad), a device the brief lists as tier-1 in its own right, distinct from 7:25's second-person commissioning charge to Ezra; the row's strongest_rejected_alternative addresses only backward attachment to 7:21-24 and never tests this interior split.
challenges.suggested_action: Add explicit reasoning for why the commission (7:25) and its general enforcement clause (7:26) form one row despite 7:26's self-contained conditional structure — e.g., argue a charge-plus-its-own-sanction is a recognized single administrative unit — rather than leaving the finer alternative untested.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the cluster's most heavily argued row and it is arguing for the right outcome, but its evidence is oddly weakened in three places. The Hebrew citations are byte-exact and correctly analysed: the blessing formula, the communal possessive, and Ezra's own 1cs onset are all present as described, and the row is right that the hinge does not simply dissolve into the register that follows. Yet the single strongest signal available at 7:27 is absent from the row's own list of co-occurring shifts, the resumption at 8:1 is reduced to an English gloss when the Hebrew shows a fuller bracket, the reason given for preferring the incipit invokes a ranking that the device matrix does not contain, and one clause is textually garbled. None of this moves the span; all of it weakens the packet at a seam the strategy already flags as low-confidence.

challenges.claim: The “co-occurring triple shift” omits the substrate change that carries the three shifts it does name. The book's second Aramaic zone closes at the end of 7:26, and 7:27 resumes in Hebrew; the language field of verse_map_oshb.json records the changeover at exactly that join, and the device matrix accordingly lists 7:27 among the 4 language-switch seams it identifies book-wide (4:8, 6:19, 7:12, 7:27), precisely because the switch there co-occurs with the blessing formula and the 1cs onset. Diction, genre and voice are each itemised in the row; the switch, which is the tier-1 driver of the seam, is absent from it.
challenges.suggested_action: Name the zone close at the head of the co-occurrence, mirror oshb:Ezra.7.26 into the boundary evidence refs beside oshb:Ezra.7.27, and reconsider confidence upward once the strongest signal is on the record.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative both undersells the echo and leans on a hierarchy that does not exist. The resumption is not merely the WEB wording “with me”: oshb:Ezra.7.28 closes לַעֲל֥וֹת עִמִּֽי and oshb:Ezra.8.1 has הָעֹלִ֣ים עִמִּ֗י — one root in an infinitive answered by a participle, carrying the identical prepositional phrase — which is a considerably stronger bracket than a shared gloss. Reducing it to the English understates the very rival the row must defeat. The stated reason for defeating it, that ranking the echo above the incipit would reverse “the device matrix's own hierarchy of tier-1 signals”, has no source: the matrix sets out era openers, document-copy formulas, register incipits, language-switch seams, person-shift seams and speech frames as co-ordinate tier-1 classes, with an ordering between tiers but none within tier 1.
challenges.suggested_action: Quote both halves of the bracket in the Hebrew — oshb:Ezra.7.28 לַעֲל֥וֹת עִמִּֽי against oshb:Ezra.8.1 הָעֹלִ֣ים עִמִּ֗י — so the rival is stated at full strength, and rest the rejection on a ground the sources actually supply — that 8:1 carries an independent opener of its own, so the echo binds the discourse without preventing a formal seam — rather than on an unstated ranking.

primary_reviews.rationale: The triple co-occurring shift at 7:27 (diction, genre, voice) is exactly right and genuinely the strongest opening signal in the cluster. This row also does work the others don't attempt: it names the strategy's own preferred forward-attachment reading, engages it directly, and argues a discourse-voice-versus-literary-form distinction to justify keeping 7:27-28 as its own row — that transparency is worth crediting. But it tests only two positions, full separation versus full merger of 7:27-28 into 8:1, and skips a position the strategy's own matrix arguably invites: the matrix keys the memoir person-shift specifically to the 7:27→7:28 transition ('doxology → אני framing'), and 7:28's closing clause functions like a frame sentence anticipating the register that follows, paralleling how 9:5's posture frame is treated as belonging with the prayer it introduces.

primary_reviews.rationale: The core of this row is right and one of its two structural claims I checked exhaustively rather than accepting: every entry from 8:3 to 8:14 does carry a headcount clause — 12 of 12 verses, each pairing a comitative phrase with a figure and the masculine plural noun (oshb:Ezra.8.4 וְעִמּ֖וֹ מָאתַ֥יִם הַזְּכָרִֽים; oshb:Ezra.8.13 וְעִמָּהֶ֖ם שִׁשִּׁ֥ים הַזְּכָרִֽים) — so 8:2's lack of one is a genuine class difference and not an impression. The 1cs anchor at 8:1 is quoted accurately, and the handling of the PE at 7:28 is exemplary: it is disclosed as belonging to the preceding part and expressly not counted as corroboration inside this span, which is how an out-of-span mark should be treated. Two of the supports nevertheless do not hold as stated. One comparandum is not the formula the row says it is, and the sweep distribution shows the formula operating at more than one level, including inside this row's own register; and the mark argument in the rival is made without the per-entry disclosure that this campaign's marker policy requires inside a list chapter.

challenges.claim: “The same formula” is not attested at 10:18. oshb:Ezra.2.1 does open וְאֵ֣לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֗ה, which matches 8:1's demonstrative plus construct chain, but oshb:Ezra.10.18 opens with a Niphal wayyiqtol, וַיִּמָּצֵא֙ מִבְּנֵ֣י הַכֹּהֲנִ֔ים, and has no demonstrative opener at all; it is a register opener of a different form. The formula is also not reserved for register onsets. sweep.py --skel ואלה: 6 occurrences book-wide, of which Ezra.6.12 is a substring artefact of the Aramaic וֵֽאלָהָ֞א, leaving 5 real tokens — 1:9, 2:1, 2:59, 8:1, 8:13 — and two of those five head sub-groups inside registers rather than registers themselves: oshb:Ezra.2.59 וְאֵ֗לֶּה הָֽעֹלִים֙ within the chapter-2 list, and oshb:Ezra.8.13 וְאֵ֣לֶּה שְׁמוֹתָ֔ם within the very register this row opens. The boundary force at 8:1 therefore comes from what is appended to the opener — the classification term וְהִתְיַחְשָׂ֑ם, the 1cs anchor הָעֹלִ֣ים עִמִּ֗י, and the regnal date — not from the demonstrative formula as such.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop 10:18 from the same-formula claim, keeping it if wanted as a register opener of different form and equal function, and rest the incipit's boundary force on 8:1's expanded elements with the sweep distribution (5 real tokens, 2 of them sub-register) disclosed.

challenges.claim: List discipline. The row cites the SAMEKH after 8:1 and the triple after 8:2 and then argues in the rival that the triple “lands on exactly the three names of 8:2 and none of the verses that follow”, without ever disclosing that a mark follows every verse of this register. pmarks_Ezra.json (single-witness) records SAMEKH after each of Ezra.8.1 through Ezra.8.13 — with SAMEKH+SAMEKH+SAMEKH at 8.2 and SAMEKH+SAMEKH at 8.3 — and PE after Ezra.8.14 — 14 of 14 verses in the register bear a mark. The marker policy requires exactly this per-entry disclosure before an entry-level samekh is used as corroboration at a sub-register seam. The triple's uniqueness is true as far as it goes, but it is a count difference inside a uniform per-entry pattern, and as written the rival invites a contrast at 8:2|8:3 that the distribution does not supply — 8:3 is itself doubly marked.
challenges.suggested_action: Disclose the full 8:1-8:14 per-entry pattern with its counts, and confine the mark argument to the correspondence between mark count and entry count within 8:2 alone; the tier-1 incipit and the absent headcount clause already carry this row without the rival's mark contrast.

primary_reviews.rationale: 8:1's register incipit sharing its opening word with 2:1 (both ואלה) is solid, directly byte-comparable tier-1 evidence, and the 8:2-versus-8:3-onward headcount-clause distinction is independently verifiable and correct — a genuinely sharp granularity argument. But the claim that this is 'the same formula the matrix attests at Ezra.2.1 and Ezra.10.18' overstates the 10:18 half of the comparison: 10:18 opens וימצא מבני הכהנים, a wayyiqtol notice-of-discovery construction sharing no lexical or morphological form with ואלה. The strategy document's own device matrix lists all three as distinct byte-verified specimens grouped under one functional heading, not as one shared formula, and this row's phrasing elides that distinction.

primary_reviews.rationale: All three sliced specimens (8:3, 8:4, 8:13) collate at byte tier, and the language zone is right: chapter 8 lies outside both Aramaic blocks, so Hebrew categories apply throughout. The register's closing element is a numeral plus the definite הַזְּכָרִֽים, which a skeleton sweep puts at 11 verses book-wide, all of them within 8:4-8:14. Verse 8:3 sits outside that set: it closes with the verbal הִתְיַחֵ֥שׂ לִזְכָרִ֖ים, and the hithpael of that root stands at 2 verses book-wide (8:1, 8:3), its partner being the incipit's וְהִתְיַחְשָׂ֑ם on the far side of this row's front seam. So the verse the row picks as its illustration is the entry that departs from the pattern it is meant to illustrate. Uniformity is loose in the leader slot too: 8:5 and 8:10 supply a patronymic with no personal name (בֶּן יַחֲזִיאֵ֑ל; בֶּן יוֹסִפְיָ֑ה). None of this sinks the span. A numbered headcount begins at 8:3 and is absent from 8:2, which is a serviceable front-seam criterion the row does not state, and the rear seam at 8:14|8:15 is clean, the register giving way to a narrative verb in Ezra's own voice. The row cites no marginal mark as evidence, and its passing description of the register's mark pattern is accurate against pmarks_Ezra.json, so no disclosure duty arises.

challenges.claim: The specimen chosen to demonstrate the entry formula is the entry that breaks it, and it breaks it in the direction of the block above the front seam (tier-1, the text's own register signals). The formula's closing element, numeral plus definite הַזְּכָרִֽים, is attested at 11 verses book-wide by skeleton sweep (8:4, 8:5, 8:6, 8:7, 8:8, 8:9, 8:10, 8:11, 8:12, 8:13, 8:14) and is absent from 8:3, which instead closes with the verbal clause הִתְיַחֵ֥שׂ לִזְכָרִ֖ים - a finite hithpael plus an indefinite prepositional phrase where the other entries have a bare numeral plus a determined noun. The hithpael of that root is attested at 2 verses book-wide by skeleton sweep, 8:1 and 8:3, so 8:3's distinctive verb is shared with the register incipit וְהִתְיַחְשָׂ֑ם and with nothing else in Ezra. Read from the Hebrew, 8:3 is a hybrid entry that leans back toward 8:1-2, which is evidence against the front seam the row inherits, not the illustration of it. The claim of uniformity also passes over 8:5 and 8:10, where the leader slot holds a patronymic and no personal name.

challenges.claim: The shape parallel drawn between 8:13 and 8:2 is inverted and does not hold. 8:2 is three separate clan entries carrying one name apiece (Phinehas/Gershom, Ithamar/Daniel, David/Hattush); 8:13 is one clan carrying three names, and those names are introduced by their own formula וְאֵ֣לֶּה שְׁמוֹתָ֔ם. Three-clans-by-one-name and one-clan-by-three-names are opposite shapes, so 8:13 does not echo 8:2. More to the point, the demonstrative incipit at 8:13 is the same lexical opener the register itself begins with at 8:1 (skeleton sweep: 6 verses book-wide - 1:9, 2:1, 2:59, 6:12, 8:1, 8:13, where the 6:12 hit is the Aramaic form for 'God' catching as a consonantal substring and is not this lexeme, leaving 5 Hebrew tokens). That makes 8:12|8:13 a live candidate sub-register seam on tier-1 grounds, and the rejected alternative waves at 8:13-14 as a possible colophon without engaging the incipit that is actually there.

primary_reviews.rationale: The row's real boundary driver is sound: 8:13's self-flagging closing word, oshb:Ezra.8.13 “אַחֲרֹנִים֒” ("the last"), is a genuine list-internal closing signal, and the count-clause survives into 8:13-14 in modified form, so the register correctly runs 8:3-14 as one entry-formula unit. The supplementary claim that 8:13 "echoes" 8:2's trio is weaker than the rest of the argument and is challenged below.

challenges.claim: The rationale calls 8:13's three names “echoing 8:2's opening trio in shape,” but the two triads aren't formally alike. 8:2 reads oshb:Ezra.8.2 “מִבְּנֵ֤י פִֽינְחָס֙ גֵּֽרְשֹׁ֔ם מִבְּנֵ֥י אִיתָמָ֖ר דָּנִיֵּ֑אל מִבְּנֵ֥י דָוִ֖יד חַטּֽוּשׁ” -- three SEPARATE patrilines (Phinehas, Ithamar, David), one leader each, with no headcount clause at all. 8:13 reads oshb:Ezra.8.13 “וּמִבְּנֵ֣י אֲדֹנִיקָם֮ אַחֲרֹנִים֒ וְאֵ֣לֶּה שְׁמוֹתָ֔ם אֱלִיפֶ֖לֶט יְעִיאֵ֣ל וּֽשְׁמַעְיָ֑ה וְעִמָּהֶ֖ם שִׁשִּׁ֥ים הַזְּכָרִֽים” -- three names under ONE patriline (Adonikam), closed by a single shared headcount ("sixty males"). The only thing the two verses share is a bare count of three personal names; the entry-formula shape (patriline count, presence or absence of a headcount clause) differs. Citing this as an "echo" implies a framing/inclusio the entry data doesn't support, even used as decoration rather than as the boundary's actual driver.
challenges.suggested_action: Drop the "echoing 8:2's opening trio in shape" clause, or reword it to concede the parallel is a bare numerical coincidence rather than a shared entry-formula shape; the closing "last" language and the surviving count-clause already carry the 8:13/8:14 argument without it.

primary_reviews.rationale: The repair retires v0's overstated "uniform entry formula" but substitutes a criterion that argues against this row's own frozen front seam. v1 defines the entry's closing element as a headcount clause "closing on numeral plus definite הַזְּכָרִֽים", then calls it "absent only from 8:2 among this register's own material, which is the actual criterion separating 8:2 from 8:3 rather than any uniformity of shape". Sweep of that element (sweep.py --heb; byte 11, skeleton 11) places it in exactly 11 verses, Ezra.8.4-Ezra.8.14 — so it is absent from 8:1, 8:2 AND 8:3 alike: 8:3 reads הִתְיַחֵ֥שׂ לִזְכָרִ֖ים (indefinite, lamed-prefixed), not the definite closing element. The false exclusivity rides on the adjacent "11 times book-wide" count, so check_universals.py passes it (re-run on this slice: 0 genuine flags). (+2 further finding(s); see challenges)

primary_reviews.rationale: Every quoted form collates at byte tier and each verb label the row uses is right in isolation: וָֽאֶקְבְּצֵ֗ם and וָאֶשְׁלְחָ֡ה are both waw-consecutive imperfects with paragogic he, and וַיָּבִ֨יאּוּ is a 3mp wayyiqtol carrying the subject switch from Ezra to the returning party. What fails is the connective claim. The clause standing between those two openers is not part of any chain: וּמִבְּנֵ֥י fronts a prepositional phrase and negates a qatal, which is a clause-type break at exactly the junction the rejected alternative wants. The row's medium_low confidence and its own admission that the seam is contested are the honest parts; the word 'unbroken' is not. Two smaller inaccuracies sit in the same sentence pair: the delegation is eleven named men rather than nine, and the verb the row's summary rests on is a ketiv/qere pair. The rear seam at 8:20|8:21 is sound - 8:21 opens a fresh 1cs act with its own purpose clauses.

challenges.claim: The stated warrant for refusing the 8:15|8:16 split misdescribes the Hebrew at that junction. 8:15 does not end in a wayyiqtol: its closing clause is וּמִבְּנֵ֥י, a fronted prepositional phrase followed by the negative and a 1cs qatal. A negated qatal after fronting is a clause-type break, and it is the rival's whole case, so saying the chain 'runs unbroken from the gathering verb that opens 8:15 through the sending verb that opens 8:16' asserts continuity across the one clause that lacks it. The defensible form of the argument is different and weaker: the chain resumes at 8:16 and the intervening break is not a tier-1 device - no era opener, no posture frame, no register incipit - so the break does not license a row edge. Strategy section 7 lists this junction among the low-confidence regions, which is where an accurate warrant matters most.
challenges.suggested_action: Replace 'unbroken' with the accurate description - a fronted negated qatal problem-notice intervenes, the wayyiqtol chain resumes at 8:16, and the break is not of a tier-1 class - and leave the residual risk to the medium_low confidence already assigned.

challenges.claim: Two factual slips in the summary of the errand. One, the count: 8:16 lists nine men closed by the apposition רָאשִׁ֑ים (Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, Meshullam) and then two more, Joiarib and Elnathan, closed by מְבִינִֽים; the party commissioned in 8:17 is therefore eleven named men, not nine. Second, the verb the phrase 'sent to Iddo' rests on is a ketiv/qere pair at 8:17, ואוצאה וָאֲצַוֶּ֤ה, the unpointed ketiv reading as a verb of sending and the pointed qere as a verb of commanding, with a second pair הנתונים הַנְּתִינִים֙ in the same verse; WEB follows the ketiv. Strategy section 4 asks for disclosure when a row leans on a ketiv/qere, and this row's characterisation of the episode leans on one.

challenges.claim: The rationale says 8:16-17 names "nine men sent... to Iddo," but the verse's single verb governs eleven, not nine: oshb:Ezra.8.16 “וָאֶשְׁלְחָ֡ה לֶאֱלִיעֶ֡זֶר לַאֲרִיאֵ֡ל לִֽ֠שְׁמַעְיָה וּלְאֶלְנָתָ֨ן וּלְיָרִ֜יב וּלְאֶלְנָתָ֧ן וּלְנָתָ֛ן וְלִזְכַרְיָ֥ה וְלִמְשֻׁלָּ֖ם רָאשִׁ֑ים וּלְיוֹיָרִ֥יב וּלְאֶלְנָתָ֖ן מְבִינִֽים” lists nine men ending in the label “וְלִמְשֻׁלָּ֖ם רָאשִׁ֑ים” ("...and Meshullam, chief men"), plus two more, “וּלְיוֹיָרִ֥יב וּלְאֶלְנָתָ֖ן מְבִינִֽים” ("and Joiarib and Elnathan, teachers"), all under the same sending verb that opens the verse. This doesn't touch the chain argument the boundary rests on, but it misdescribes the headcount of the very verse (8:16) the row leans on as core evidence.

primary_reviews.rationale: The three quotations collate at byte tier and the internal analysis of the unit is sound: וָאֶקְרָ֨א opens a fresh 1cs act, 8:22 is a causal clause headed by the particle plus the 1cs qatal בֹ֗שְׁתִּי which embeds a further quotation frame, and וַנָּצ֛וּמָה וַנְּבַקְשָׁ֥ה reports the result, sealed by וַיֵּעָתֵ֖ר. challenges.claim: The stated close-warrant is unavailable because the row's own span falsifies it. The verbal persons run: 8:21 וָאֶקְרָ֨א (1cs), 8:22 בֹ֗שְׁתִּי (1cs) beside אָמַ֨רְנוּ (1cp), 8:23 וַנָּצ֛וּמָה וַנְּבַקְשָׁ֥ה (1cp), then 8:24 וָאַבְדִּ֛ילָה (1cs). A 1cs-to-1cp alternation that the row treats as inert twice within three verses cannot carry a boundary at its third occurrence; 'Ezra alone acting rather than the assembled we' describes 8:21 as accurately as it describes 8:24. What does hold at 8:23|8:24 is a completed request-and-answer shape - proclamation, causal motive, result clause וַיֵּעָתֵ֖ר - followed by an unrelated administrative act.
challenges.suggested_action: Rest the rear edge on the closure of the fast's own petition-and-answer shape and on the new administrative topic at 8:24, and drop the person-shift argument, which the row's interior contradicts.

challenges.claim: The rejected alternative faces backward while the harder rival faces forward. Nothing in the Hebrew changes place or speaker between 8:21 and 8:30: the fast is proclaimed at the river (8:21) and the caravan is still there when it leaves at 8:31, מִנְּהַ֣ר אַֽהֲוָ֗א, so 8:21-30 is readable as one pre-departure block at Ahava in Ezra's 1cs voice, bounded by the arrival notice at 8:15 and the departure notice at 8:31. That rival is stronger than the backward attachment the row rejects, because the backward attachment has to cross the recruitment result (8:18-20) whose 3mp subject differs from everything around it, whereas the forward rival crosses nothing but a change of topic. Since the row's stated rear-edge warrant does not survive (see OL-M8-Ezra-043-1), the forward rival is the one that needs answering.
challenges.suggested_action: Add or substitute the forward attachment 8:21-30 as the strongest rejected alternative and say what makes the fast and the custody transfer two acts rather than one preparation block.

primary_reviews.rationale: Quotes collate at byte tier and the inset call is right for the reason given: וָאֹמְרָ֣ה אֲלֵהֶ֗ם opens the charge, and nothing closes it - there is no 'when he had finished speaking' formula, so the speech has a single frame and stays with its host scene, matching how the strategy handles the posture-framed prayer later in the book. Worth recording that the narrative resumes at 8:30 with וְקִבְּלוּ֙, a waw plus piel perfect rather than a wayyiqtol; this is the late-Hebrew narrative continuation, not a resumptive formula, so it does not supply the second frame the inset rule would require for a split, which if anything confirms the row's call. The custody vocabulary is continuous across the span (skeleton sweep on the weighing root: 6 verses book-wide - 8:25, 8:26, 8:29, 8:30, 8:33, 8:34; the 8:25 hit rides the qere, its ketiv ואשקולה carrying an infixed mater that a contiguous consonantal search does not match). Personnel, by contrast, are not continuous, and the rejected alternative leans on them.

challenges.claim: 'The same twelve officials and the same treasure run continuously across the span' overstates what the Hebrew supports on the personnel side. 8:24 sets apart twelve מִשָּׂרֵ֥י הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים and names לְשֵׁרֵֽבְיָ֣ה חֲשַׁבְיָ֔ה, yet the same memoir a few verses earlier placed Sherebiah among the sons of Mahli son of Levi (8:18) and Hashabiah with Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari (8:19), which are Levitical lines, not priestly ones. The charge at 8:29 then anticipates a deposit before שָׂרֵ֨י הַכֹּהֲנִ֧ים וְהַלְוִיִּ֛ם, and the subject that actually receives at 8:30 is the two-class collective הַכֹּהֲנִ֣ים וְהַלְוִיִּ֔ם, not a resumption of the twelve. Participant identity is therefore an open question inside this span rather than a premise available to the unit-integrity argument.
challenges.suggested_action: Rest the continuity claim on the weighing chain, which is verifiable and unbroken, and restate the personnel point as designations that shift across the span (twelve chiefs of the priests, then priests and Levites) rather than as sameness.

primary_reviews.rationale: Pressed on why the inset rule is applied to an ordinary charge speech (8:28-29) rather than to a formally marked document, since strategy §2's specimens are edicts, letters, and a prayer. The distinction holds up: unlike 043's proclamation, which opens a genuinely new topic and addressee, 8:28's charge keeps the same twelve officials and the same treasure inside one uninterrupted administrative transaction (set apart -> weigh -> charge -> receive), with no resumption frame marking it off. That is a defensible, non-arbitrary application of the rule, not a stretch.

The repair rightly retires the "same twelve officials" cohesion warrant, but the replacement — "Unit integrity rests instead on the weighing vocabulary, which does run continuously and verifiably across the span" — fails on both halves of that sentence. Sweep of the weighing root returns exactly 6 verses book-wide: 8:25, 8:26, 8:29, 8:30, 8:33, 8:34. Inside this row's 7-verse span the root is absent from 8:24, 8:27 and 8:28 — the row's own opening verse, the last itemisation verse, and the opening of the charge — so "continuously ... across the span" overstates a run that covers 4 of 7 verses; and 2 of the 6 sit in the FOLLOWING row, so the run cannot discriminate 8:24-30 from 8:24-34. The neighbouring row M8-Ezra-045 in this same slice reaches exactly that verdict about the same run ("citing it as an inclusio closing THIS row would claim a frame that in fact cuts across the 8:30/8:31 join"), while this row rests its unit integrity on it; the partial hedge here ("part of a book-wide bracket the next row's verification completes") acknowledges the overrun without letting it modify the claim. challenges.claim: The row calls the custody link an inclusio, but an inclusio delimits a unit, and this one delimits 8:24-34, straddling the row's own front seam at 8:30|8:31. primary_reviews.rationale: Both quotations collate at byte tier, and the front seam this row asserts is genuinely strong - stronger than the row argues. 8:35 begins הַ֠בָּאִים, a determined participle with no conjunction at all, apposed to בְנֵֽי הַגּוֹלָ֜ה and completed by the qatal הִקְרִ֥יבוּ; an asyndetic fronted participial subject taking a suffix-conjugation verb is a clause-type break, which is a better warrant than the subject-change the row names. challenges.claim: Tier-3 disclosure in this row is one-sided. Citing the mark after 8:34 as the front seam and the mark after 8:36 as the rear seam while passing over an interior mark of the same PE class (single-witness) is the selective disclosure the marker policy forbids, and it is selective in the direction that favours the row: the omitted mark is weak corroboration for the split being refused. It also slipped through the tooling. The symmetry rule in check_marks.py accepts any mark word within 160 characters of a mention of the verse, and the string 8:35 in the rejected-alternative sentence happens to fall that close to the PE (single-witness) claim made about 8:34, so the row passes on proximity rather than on an actual disclosure. This does not touch the span itself - a marker claim can neither drive nor defeat a boundary - but the disclosure record is wrong.

challenges.claim: 'Ezra.8.36 continues the same vav-consecutive chain' has no antecedent chain to refer to. 8:35 opens with הַ֠בָּאִים - a definite participle carrying no conjunction - and its finite verb is the qatal הִקְרִ֥יבוּ; there is no waw-consecutive form anywhere in the verse. 8:36's וַֽיִּתְּנ֣וּ is a wayyiqtol, so it begins a sequence rather than continuing one, and a wayyiqtol following a fronted-subject qatal clause is ordinary consecution, which is all the rejected alternative actually needs. The correction helps the row twice over: it removes a grammatical mislabel, and the asyndetic participial opening it exposes is a stronger front-seam signal at 8:34|8:35 than the change of acting subject the row relies on.

primary_reviews.rationale: The seam at 9:1 is real and I do not contest the span: a temporal clause opens the verse, the participant field changes as officials approach Ezra, and a speech frame follows. The row's argumentation, though, carries three original-language defects, which matters because its Hebrew evidence amounts to the opener, two single words, and the closing clause. The mislabelling of אֵלַ֤י is the clearest: it is the preposition with a 1cs suffix governed by the niphal נִגְּשׁ֨וּ, not an object marker. The extent of the quoted report is argued from the translation's punctuation rather than from Hebrew, and the Hebrew has a complication the row does not record. And the opener is classed as an era formula though it carries nothing calendrical, with a literal gloss that passivises a D-stem infinitive. All four sliced forms collate at byte tier and the verses are Hebrew, outside both Aramaic zones, so Hebrew categories are the right ones here.

challenges.claim: Grammatical mislabel: אֵלַ֤י is not an object marker. It is the preposition meaning 'to' with the 1cs suffix, serving as the complement of the verb of approach נִגְּשׁ֨וּ (niphal qatal 3cp), with הַשָּׂרִים֙ as the subject that follows it. Hebrew's object marker is the particle seen at 9:3 in אֶת הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה, which is a different word entirely and does not occur in 9:1-2. The evidential point the row wants - that Ezra becomes the addressee - survives the correction, but in a row whose original-language footing is this narrow, a wrong part-of-speech label on one of its four cited forms is not cosmetic.
challenges.suggested_action: Restate as: the prepositional phrase, complement of the verb of approach, makes Ezra the addressee, and the speech is introduced by the infinitive לֵאמֹ֔ר.

challenges.claim: The rear edge is carried by translator's punctuation, and the Hebrew complicates the claim it is used to make. 'WEB's quotation opens at ... and the princes' report runs as one uninterrupted quotation through 9:2's close' rests on quotation marks, which belong to the translation's formatting, the tier-4 class; the Hebrew supplies a speech-onset infinitive with no closing counterpart anywhere in 9:2. Meanwhile the participant terms cut across the quotation as delimited: the speakers at 9:1 are הַשָּׂרִים֙ and the group indicted at the end of 9:2 is הַשָּׂרִ֣ים וְהַסְּגָנִ֗ים (skeleton sweep on the noun: 4 verses book-wide - 8:20, 9:1, 9:2, 10:8), so the report as bounded has the reporting officials denouncing their own class in the third person. That is a real feature of the text and it should be stated, not smoothed into 'one uninterrupted quotation'. The seam is better carried from the Hebrew side: 9:3's anaphoric object phrase אֶת הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה looks back over the whole report and closes it, and the narration returns to 1cs.
challenges.suggested_action: Argue the 9:2|9:3 close from the anaphoric object phrase at 9:3 plus the return to 1cs narration; downgrade the punctuation argument to a note; and disclose the third-person self-reference of the reporting officials instead of asserting an uninterrupted report.
